title: Sense and Sensibility
description: A social novel of two orphaned sisters, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, who illustrate contrasting regimes of feeling and judgement after being displaced from their father's estate. The work grew out of an epistolary juvenile experiment of the late 1790s and was reworked into a third-person narrative of discretion, disappointment and eventual settlement. Its argument is not that sensibility is false but that unexamined feeling needs the discipline of principle.
plot_or_argument: Sir John Dashwood, influenced by his wife Fanny, keeps the promised provision from his stepmother and half-sisters, who remove to a cottage on the estate of a distant relation. Marianne attaches herself passionately to the charming, impecunious John Willoughby, who is recalled to London and marries a rich heiress instead; Elinor quietly endures the secret engagement of her own beloved Edward Ferrars to the artful Lucy Steele. Marianne's exposed grief carries her to illness and near death, while Edward is disinherited for honouring his early pledge and is only freed when Lucy transfers herself to his brother. The novel closes with double marriages, Marianne's cooler second choice of the steady Colonel Brandon, and a modest restoration of family order.
narrative_structure: Third-person narration with sustained free indirect discourse anchored now in Elinor and now in Marianne; linear, episodic plot of removals between Devonshire, Sussex, London and Cleveland; letters and reported conversation carry offstage information.
principal_characters: Elinor Dashwood; Marianne Dashwood; Edward Ferrars; Colonel Brandon; John Willoughby; Mrs. Jennings; Lucy Steele; Fanny Dashwood; Sir John Dashwood; Mrs. Dashwood; Robert Ferrars
literary_form: Novel of manners and domestic moral comedy, inheriting the 1790s vogue for the fiction of sensibility while inverting it through irony and conditional endings.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; balanced periodic sentences, epigrammatic dialogue, and a famous antithetical title-phrase in iambic rhythm.
historical_context: Written through the 1790s controversy over sensibility and the education of women, and revised during the Napoleonic Wars when the commercial and clerical careers open to gentle families were precarious. The novel's entailed estates, half-pay officers and drawing-room politics register the specific economic vulnerability of the landless gentry. It was offered to a London publisher at a moment when the three-volume novel had become a financial as well as a literary form.
literary_significance: The first work of the school of social realism that displaced the romance of sensibility, and the founding text of the novel of manners in the Regency mode. Its treatment of female feeling as both social currency and private suffering set the terms for later women's fiction. Its revision from epistolary draft to narrated tale is a documented case of 1790s experimental form being absorbed into nineteenth-century realism.
attribution_notes: Published as 'By A Lady'; identification of the author rests on publisher's records and family documentation and is not in dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1811, in three volumes, by T. Egerton, styled 'By A Lady'; the manuscript is not preserved. Standard scholarly text is the Cambridge/Northanger Abbey edition based on the first edition.

title: Pride and Prejudice
description: The most widely read English novel of the marriage market: a comedy of misjudgement in which the quick-witted Elizabeth Bennet and the proud landowner Fitzwilliam Darcy must each revise their first readings of the other. Drafted rapidly in the mid-1790s as First Impressions and revised a dozen years later, it perfects the ironic narration of a heroine learning to distrust her own sagacity. Its social field is the country town and the county assembly, where rank, fortune and accomplishment are endlessly weighed.
plot_or_argument: The arrival of the wealthy bachelor Bingley at Netherfield sets the five Bennet sisters in motion; Jane draws his attachment while Elizabeth forms an unfavourable judgement of his friend Darcy, reinforced by the handsome officer George Wickham. Darcy proposes despite his objections to her family and is refused with fury; his written vindication of himself, and his secret interference on her family's behalf after Lydia's elopement, reverse her opinion. Elizabeth rejects the obsequious clergyman Mr. Collins and the proud offer of her cousin's patronage, and accepts Darcy after the regaining of Lydia and the reconciliation of the two households.
narrative_structure: Third-person ironic narration focalised chiefly through Elizabeth, with strategic restriction of information; letters (Darcy's long letter, Mrs. Gardiner's accounts) act as the machinery of revelation; symmetrical proposal scenes form the structural hinge.
principal_characters: Elizabeth Bennet; Fitzwilliam Darcy; Jane Bennet; Charles Bingley; Mr. Bennet; Mrs. Bennet; Mr. Collins; Charlotte Lucas; George Wickham; Lydia Bennet; Lady Catherine de Bourgh; Mrs. Gardiner
literary_form: Comedy of manners and novel of character; two-plot comic structure in which the marriage plot is also a moral education.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; epigrammatic balanced sentences ('It is a truth universally acknowledged'), colloquial dialogue, and quoted letters in a more formal register.
historical_context: Composed in the decade of the French Wars and revised after 1811, when paper, copyright and the triple-decker system had made the novel a substantial commercial property. Its militia encampments, its anxiety about female dependence, and its estate arithmetic of four and ten thousand a year reflect the specific insecurities of the propertied classes under prolonged war. The absence of overt political reference is itself a historical effect of a novelist writing for a readership suspicious of Jacobin fiction.
literary_significance: Established the model of the novel of manners with a first-rate ironic intelligence at its centre, and the most continuously imitated plot pattern in English fiction. Its account of self-knowledge through social humiliation made it a touchstone for later realist and feminist criticism. It is the standard example of the 1790s experimental juvenile novel matured into nineteenth-century form.
attribution_notes: Advertised as 'By the author of Sense and Sensibility'; no dispute over authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1813, in three volumes, by T. Egerton; a second edition appeared the same year. Revised from an early draft written in 1796-97; the working manuscript of the 1813 text survives fragmentarily.

title: Mansfield Park
description: The most morally severe of the early nineteenth-century English novels of manners, following Fanny Price, a poor relation boarded in her uncle's baronetcy, from the Portsmouth slums to a West Indian estate and back. The novel tests principle against charm, and makes the theatre, the improvement of grounds and the question of colonial wealth matters of explicit argument. Its quiet heroine's steadfastness has made it the most debated of her works.
plot_or_argument: Fanny Price, sent at twelve to live with her wealthy relatives at Mansfield Park, loves her cousin Edmund and is loved in return by her uncle's circle, but is dispatched home to her disorderly Portsmouth family when her aunt hopes to marry her off. The arrival of the charismatic Crawfords breaks the household's decorum: brother and sister both court Fanny while pursuing her cousins, and a private theatricals scheme is only halted by her uncle's return. Fanny refuses the importunate Henry Crawford on principle; his elopement with Maria Rushworth exposes the corruption she had distrusted, and Edmund's settlement on a living, with a slow marriage to Fanny, closes the tale. The final paragraphs remark that the colonies were the source of the family's income and that its management was not in sympathetic hands.
narrative_structure: Third-person narration tightly focalised through Fanny, whose limited access and prolonged silence generate the novel's suspense; framed by a summarising conclusion that reports the later lives of the characters.
principal_characters: Fanny Price; Edmund Bertram; Sir Thomas Bertram; Lady Bertram; Tom Bertram; Maria Bertram; Julia Bertram; Henry Crawford; Mary Crawford; Mrs. Norris; Mr. Rushworth; Susan Price
literary_form: Domestic and sentimental novel of manners with a static moral centre; a country-house plot combined with didactic debate about acting, clergy and improvement.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a more formal, latinate diction than the earlier novels, with heavy use of reported speech and moral tag.
historical_context: Written during the Peninsular War, when the Antiguan slavery and sugar interests that fund the Bertram estate were a live parliamentary issue and when the abolitionist cause was dividing families of the kind depicted. The campaign against private theatricals reflects the evangelical and clerical scrutiny of the stage then reshaping polite amusement. The novel's language of 'improvements' and 'living' belongs to the agrarian and clerical debates of the Regency decade.
literary_significance: The most serious attempt in the school of manners to make moral principle, rather than wit, the subject of a novel, and the source of the long critical quarrel about whether Fanny's passivity is virtue or self-suppression. Its treatment of colonial income makes it a focal text for postcolonial readings of the Regency novel. Its influence on the later domestic novel of conscience is extensive.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously as by the author of the preceding novels; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1814, in three volumes, by Thomas Egerton; second edition 1816. Working manuscript survives at the British Library.

title: Emma
description: A comic novel of a self-sufficient young gentlewoman who mistakes her own discernment for a right to arrange other people's lives, written in a deliberately narrower style than its predecessors: 'three or four families in a country village'. The plot is a slow education of the imagination in which every act of matchmaking is a misreading, and the discovery of the heroine's own feeling for Mr. Knightley arrives as surprise to her and to the reader. It is the most technically self-conscious of the Regency novels of manners.
plot_or_argument: Emma Woodhouse, having persuaded her former governess to marry and resolved to continue as an amateur of destinies, takes the pretentious Harriet Smith as her project, discourages her from a respectable farmer's suit, and imagines her fit for the vain vicar Mr. Elton. The vicar's unexpected advance on Emma herself explodes the scheme, and the arrival of the lively, mysterious Frank Churchill, long linked by rumour to Jane Fairfax, generates a second set of false readings until the secret engagement of the two is disclosed. A botched picnic at Box Hill exposes Emma's cruelty to the dependent Miss Bates and draws from Mr. Knightley the rebuke that becomes the novel's moral centre; Harriet's alarming encounter with gypsies confirms Emma in her errors, and Knightley's jealousy of Churchill reveals the attachment Emma has never perceived in herself. Harriet is redirected to a suitable partner, Jane Fairfax married in secret no longer, and Emma united to Knightley with her father accommodated in the two families' shared household.
narrative_structure: Free indirect discourse carried further than in any earlier novel, so that the narration is coloured by Emma's errors and the reader shares her limited knowledge; long set-piece scenes (the ball, Box Hill) supply the plot's turning points.
principal_characters: Emma Woodhouse; Mr. Knightley; Harriet Smith; Mr. Woodhouse; Frank Churchill; Jane Fairfax; Mr. Elton; Mrs. Elton; Miss Bates; Mrs. Weston; Colonel and Mrs. Campbell
literary_form: Comedy of manners and novel of moral education; an inversion of the conduct-plot in which the heroine's imagination, not her circumstances, is the obstacle.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; dry, clipped sentence rhythms, with irony largely produced by reported thought rather than narrator comment.
historical_context: Written in the last years of the Napoleonic Wars and published after Waterloo, its village of Highbury is an image of an England insulated from the continent; the elopement of Harriet with the gypsy band, which never happened, is a parody of Gothic plots still circulating in the periodical fiction of the 1810s. Its social anxieties about the Gentleman's class, the genteel spinster and the professional dentist belong to the expanding Regency middle rank. It was dedicated, at a command performance of sorts, to the Prince Regent's circle through the intervention of his librarian.
literary_significance: The most complete realisation of the technique of ironic free indirect discourse, and a decisive model for the later novel of limited consciousness. Its treatment of a woman's imagination as a moral problem, and of marriage as a settlement of class as well as feeling, has made it central to feminist and historicist criticism. It is also the period's most explicit theorising of the novel of ordinary life in its own metacommentary about length and attention.
attribution_notes: Published as 'By the author of Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice, &c.'; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, December 1815, in three volumes, by John Murray, with a title page dated 1816; a second edition with a corrected text appeared the same year. The complete working manuscript is preserved.

title: Northanger Abbey
description: A comic satire on the Gothic novel and on the heroine formed by reading it, drafted in the late 1798-99 as Susan and revised a few years before its posthumous appearance. Its heroine, Catherine Morland, goes from a Bristol pump-room to a Wiltshire abbey and invents a mystery of murder and concealment where there is only a plain domestic history. The work contains the period's most quoted defence of the novel as a form and a sustained parody of the conventions of terror.
plot_or_argument: Catherine Morland, a plain and lively girl, is taken into fashionable Bath society by the well-meaning Mrs. Allen, learns to dance, and is encouraged in her hopes by the agreeable son of the master of Northanger Abbey. Reading the novels of the gothic school on the way to the Abbey, she transmutes a locked drawer, a blank manuscript and a curt question into evidence of a murdered wife and a concealed crime; the discovery that her reading has misled her is the novel's turning point, though General Tilney's pride and avarice prove all too real when he turns her from the house. The betrayal of her friend Isabella, who jilts Catherine's brother for a wealthy baronet and is then discarded, exposes the corruptions that Gothic plot-work disguises, and the concluding reconciliation with Henry Tilney arrives with an unromantic irony about the hero's prospects.
narrative_structure: Third-person narration with a self-conscious, addressing narrator, including an apologia for the novel in the opening book; a double structure of Bath society comedy and abbey parody, joined by Catherine's misreadings.
principal_characters: Catherine Morland; Henry Tilney; General Tilney; Eleanor Tilney; Isabella Thorpe; John Thorpe; James Thorpe; Mrs. Allen; Mr. Allen; Mr. Morland; Mrs. Morland
literary_form: Comic novel of manners and parody of the Gothic romance of terror; a bildungsroman of reading.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; light, rapid sentences, with parody pitched at the long trailing syntax of romance.
historical_context: Conceived when the gothic bestseller and the circulating library had made terror a staple, and revised at the end of the period when that staple was being superseded; its Bath sections record the etiquette of the water-cure crowd and its ending a war-office patronage and a marriage into the naval interest. The novel's sale to a publisher in 1803 and its non-appearance for fourteen years is a documented instance of the period's unstable copyright trade.
literary_significance: The most sustained novelised critique of Gothic reading in English, and one of the earliest defences of the novel as an art; its parody of the pursued-heroine plot helped to end that plot's reign. It is also a key document for the history of women's reading and of circulating-library culture. Its posthumous publication made its author a named presence in the early nineteenth-century canon.
attribution_notes: Published posthumously with a biographical notice by a relative; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: Written 1798-99 as Susan and sold to a publisher in 1803 who did not print it; first published December 1817 with a companion volume, the four-volume set carrying title pages dated 1818, London, John Murray. Standard edition follows the first printed text.

title: Persuasion
description: The last completed novel, a mature and lyrical story of a woman who was persuaded nearly nine years before to break off her engagement to a poor naval lieutenant, now rich and successful, and who must decide whether his wounded pride can be forgiven. Its baronet and admiral world, its impaired gentry and its rising naval wealth make it the most historically explicit of the early nineteenth-century novels of manners. The prose is more relaxed, more feeling-led, and more openly autobiographical in its predicament than anything in the earlier work.
plot_or_argument: Sir Walter Elliot, extravagant and vain, is persuaded by his steward's arithmetic to retrench and to let Kellynch Hall to Admiral Croft, whose wife is the sister of the very captain now returned from war. Anne Elliot, who nine years earlier gave way to Lady Russell's warning against the impecunious young Frederick Wentworth, is drawn back into his society at Uppercross and at Lyme, where Louisa Musgrove's fall from the Cobb throws the family into confusion and opens Wentworth's admiration for the lively, injured girl. The baronet's grasping cousin Mr. Elliott, who courts Anne only as a possible heiress, is exposed and banished; Louisa recovers to be betrothed to the mourning Captain Benwick; and at Bath a design to attach Wentworth to the fashionable Lady Dalrymple miscarries. Anne's overheared speech on the constancy of women, followed by the interrupted conversation at the Bell, produces Wentworth's letter, and a private marriage against the wishes of her family.
narrative_structure: Third-person narration centred on Anne Elliot, with a double movement of stillness and delayed disclosure; reported conversation, overheard speech and a central letter carry the crisis; an abandoned earlier version ('Volume the First') of the same tale survives.
principal_characters: Anne Elliot; Captain Frederick Wentworth; Sir Walter Elliot; Elizabeth Elliot; Lady Dalrymple; Mrs. Clay; Admiral Croft; Mrs. Croft; Lady Russell; Mr. Musgrove; Mrs. Musgrove; Louisa Musgrove; Captain Benwick; Captain Harville; Charles Hayter; Mr. Elliott
literary_form: Novel of manners with elegiac and romantic inflection; an early example of the second-chance love plot treated as moral history.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; longer, more suspended periods than the earlier novels, with the quoted verse of the period (a ballad of the constancy theme) embedded in the text.
historical_context: Written in the immediate aftermath of Waterloo, when the naval officers who had made fortunes and reputations were entering the landed families by marriage, and the old baronetcy was visibly losing its social monopoly. Its Lyme, Bath and country-seat geography maps the post-war circulation of naval capital. It was published with a companion volume after the author's death, prefaced by a family memoir.
literary_significance: Regarded as the most moving and least schematic of the early nineteenth-century comedies of manners, and the fullest period expression of the ideology of constancy in female feeling. Its treatment of age, regret and the second chance opened a line of later realist fiction. The surviving double version of the ending is one of the most studied documents of the period's novel-writing process.
attribution_notes: Published posthumously; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: Completed August 1816, with an earlier version ('Volume the First') and an alternate conclusion preserved in the author's manuscripts; first published London, December 1817, with a companion volume in four volumes total, John Murray, title pages dated 1818.

title: Lady Susan
description: A short novel entirely in letters, dominated by a beautiful, penniless and unscrupulous widow who secures a home with her estranged in-laws, attaches their brother-in-law to herself, and markets her daughter to the richest suitor she can trap. It is the most ruthless and least reconciliatory of the early epistolary fictions of the period, and the only completed novel of its school to give the whole stage to a heroine-villain. The fair-copy manuscript in the author's hand survives.
plot_or_argument: Lady Susan Vernon, having compromised herself in London by an intimacy with the married Mr. Manwaring, retreats to the country house of her late husband's brother, Mr. Vernon, where she flatters and plunders the credulous Sir James Martin and captivates his young kinsman Reginald De Courcy. Her daughter, the gentle Catherine, whom she means to foist upon Sir James for a dowry, is taken into the family's protection and forms friendships that defeat her mother's plan. When Manwaring's jealous husband exposes the correspondence, Lady Susan abandons Reginald, extorts a settlement for herself, and at the end marries the elderly Mr. Vernon, whose estate she will command.
narrative_structure: Complete epistolary form: letters, notes and memoranda exchanged among Lady Susan, her confidante Mrs. Johnson, Catherine, De Courcy and the Manwarings, with the reader largely at the mercy of a manipulative correspondent; a brief documentary conclusion rounds the plot.
principal_characters: Lady Susan Vernon; Frederica Vernon; Reginald De Courcy; Mr. Vernon; Mrs. Johnson; Sir James Martin; Mr. Manwaring; Mrs. Manwaring; Alice Woodford
literary_form: Epistolary novel of conduct and dissembling, inheriting the eighteenth-century letter-novel and turning it against the sentimental use of the form.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; the style differentiates characters by their letters, from Lady Susan's studied blandishment to the blunt remonstrance of the country gentry.
historical_context: Written in the years of the author's earliest maturity, when the letter-novel was being displaced by narrated realism and when the dependence of widows and unmarried women on male property was the dominant plot problem of women's fiction. Its cynicism about the marriage market belongs to the 1790s reaction against the doctrine of sensibility. The work remained in family hands for three quarters of a century and reached print only as an appendix to a biographical memoir.
literary_significance: An important document of the transition from epistolary to narrated fiction, and one of the very few early nineteenth-century novels wholly controlled by a manipulative female protagonist. Its unfinished, unrepentant ending makes it a constant subject of editorial and feminist discussion. The survival of the fair-copy manuscript gives it exceptional value for the study of the period's composing habits.
attribution_notes: Authorship established by the manuscript and family tradition; no serious dispute.
bibliographical_notes: The untitled fair-copy manuscript is preserved; first printed posthumously in 1871 as an appendix to a family memoir, and not issued as a separate book until the twentieth century. No first-performance or contemporary print record exists.

title: Love and Freindship
description: A burlesque epistolary tale of juvenile sensibility, written for family entertainment and headed 'Written at the Age of 14', in which every convention of the sentimental novel is pushed to absurdity. Its heroine narrates her own trials in a style of exhausted rapture, collapsing, eloping, disinheriting and weeping through a series of improbabilities. The surviving notebook copy preserves the author's original spelling of the title.
plot_or_argument: Laura, an orphan left with an unkind guardian, falls in love with Edward, his son, and is banished; her friend Marianne, rich and self-dramatising, alternately supports and abandons her. Patrons, elopements and revivals of fortune succeed one another without pause, and feeling itself is treated as a physical malady producing fainting, delirium, loss of property and rapid recovery. The tale closes in marriages and a general reconciliation of the sentimental plot machinery, with the correspondents comfortably supplied with income.
narrative_structure: A novel in a series of letters, with abrupt recapitulations and a self-conscious narrator who comments on the speed of her own sufferings; the parody depends on the gap between the letter-writer's rhetoric and the triviality of the events reported.
principal_characters: Laura, the self-dramatising heroine-narrator; Marianne, her friend and correspondent; Edward, her guardian's son; Sir Edward, a rival suitor of sentimental rhetoric
literary_form: Juvenilia burlesque and epistolary parody of the novel of sensibility.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; deliberately over-wrought sentimental diction with mock-heroic exaggeration, the notebooks also preserving accompanying verse fragments.
historical_context: Composed in the family reading circle of the late 1780s and early 1790s, when circulating-library fiction of feeling was at its height and parody of it was a household amusement. The manuscript belonged to a set of exercise and tale notebooks circulated among siblings and copied out for entertainment. It was not offered for publication and remained in private hands.
literary_significance: The earliest substantial evidence of a school of ironic treatment of sensibility that would mature into the regulated irony of the published novels. As a manuscript culture document it is much cited in studies of juvenile writing, family circulation and women's reading in the 1790s. Its survival lets scholars trace the making of a mature narrative voice from parody.
attribution_notes: Authorship established by the manuscript notebooks; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: Preserved in the first of the surviving tale notebooks; publication date left null because the tale appeared only posthumously in a twentieth-century scholarly edition of the early writings, whose precise imprint is not asserted here.

title: Waverley; or, 'Tis Sixty Years Since
description: The first historical novel in English, presented as a recovered memoir of the previous century and prefaced by an advertisement on the art of fabricating such a tale. Its young English officer hero, caught between the rival claims of Hanover and Jacobite Scotland during the '45, becomes the model for the neutral witness who moves between two worlds and two codes of honour. The book's anonymous appearance, and the pseudonymous 'Author of Waverley' it created, made publishing history.
plot_or_argument: Edward Waverley, a sentimental young Englishman attached to his Tory cousin the Baron of Bradwardine, is sent to a Border castle, is captured on suspicion, and falls under the spell of the Highland chieftain Fergus Mac-Ivor and his sister Flora. He joins the rising, is trusted by Prince Charles, and duels his patron's kinsman; meanwhile the Baron's estates are sequestrated and Bradwardine's chivalric logic collapses before the fact of defeat. Waverley's English protector Colonel Talbot obtains his pardon; he visits Edinburgh and London, refuses preferment, and marries the Baron's daughter Rose, while the concluding chapters and notes record the extinguishing of the patriarchal law of the Highlands.
narrative_structure: First-person framed memoir in fifty chapters with an 'Introductory Chapter' on the principles of romance and a postscript of explanatory notes; the narrator's hindsight, classical allusion and marginal learning constitute the historical perspective.
principal_characters: Edward Waverley; the Baron of Bradwardine; Rose Bradwardine; Fergus Mac-Ivor; Flora Mac-Ivor; Davie Gellatley; Colonel Talbot; Donald Bean Lean
literary_form: Historical novel and romance of civil war; a society-novel of manners transplanted into the recent past, with ballad and antiquarian apparatus.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre, with inserted verse, song fragments and quoted ballad and Latin tags.
historical_context: Begun during the Napoleonic Wars and completed while the British state was mobilising against France, it revisits the last civil war on British soil at the exact moment when Highland and Border cultures were being documented, enclosed and recruited. Publication was delayed by the author's fear of being identified as a poet, and the novel appeared anonymously when paper and copyright conditions favoured the triple-decker. Its dialect, law and theology are drawn from the antiquarian collection work of the preceding decade.
literary_significance: Founded the historical novel as a major European form and set the template of the neutral hero who mediates between opposed cultures and epochs. Its mixture of romance, ballad, footnote and sociological explanation defined the mode later writers imitated and criticised. The commercial and pseudonymous history of the book changed the economics and the authorship conventions of the nineteenth-century novel.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; the author's identity was public within months and was formally acknowledged in the 1829-30 collected edition, for which a first-person Memoir and Introduction were prefixed.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London, 1814, in three volumes, printed by James Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Co. and for Longman, Hurst, Rees and Orme, London; second edition 1814.

title: Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer
description: The second tale of the new school of Scottish fiction, a romance of Borders gentry, smuggling and legal fraud in which the fortunes of a family are read in advance by an astrological prediction. A colonel from India, quartered at a Border inn, becomes the witness and friend of the heir who had been carried off in childhood, and the tale's curiosity is sustained by the concealment of that identity. Its portraits of a sour landlady, a starved pedant and a terrier-fancier became some of the most reproduced types of Scottish popular fiction.
plot_or_argument: Colonel Mannering, seeking a lodging in the south of Scotland, is warned by an astrologer's figure of the child then missing from the neighbouring house; the infant heir Bertram had been abstracted in his mother's chamber years before, and his kinsman Glossin, the heir presumptive, had profited by the loss. Bertram returns unknown to himself, takes a farm under another name, and is entangled with the smuggler Hatteraick and with the treachery of Glossin's factor. Meg Dods, the innkeeper who loves him spitefully, Dominie Sampson, the scholar whom a marriage would starve, and Dandie Dinmont, whose puppies end the quarrels of the county, carry the novel's comedy. Detection, a trial at the circuit court and a recovery of name and estate bring the prediction to its fulfilment.
narrative_structure: Third-person narrative with Colonel Mannering as the chief intelligence-gathering witness; a large cast observed through dialect talk; a concluding assembly of evidence in court supplies the discovery of the lost heir.
principal_characters: Colonel Guy Mannering; Henry Bertram, the lost heir; Glossin, the heir presumptive; Hatteraick the smuggler; Dominie Sampson; Meg Dods; Dandie Dinmont; Julia Mannering; the astrologer
literary_form: Historical novel and romance of Border society with a strong comic and dialect component; the mystery of identity gives it an early detection plot.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; heavy use of Scots speech for the servant and border characters, with songs and ballad tags interpolated.
historical_context: Written in the same season as the author's antiquarian work on Border legends, and dependent on the record of smuggling along the Solway coast and of the civil law of entail and hypothec then being modernised. The East India interest represented by the colonel reflects the returns of Anglo-Indian wealth into Scottish land. Its publication, within months of the former tale, created the commercial pattern of the anonymous national series.
literary_significance: Established the second, comic-native mode of the historical novel and supplied the period's stock of Scottish character types. Its treatment of stolen inheritance and legal title made it a source for later sensation and detection plotting. Its dialect comedy was widely imitated and remains a document of Scots speech at the Union.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously as by the Author of Waverley; attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London, December 1815, in three volumes, printed by James Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Co.; a second edition followed in 1815-16.

title: The Antiquary
description: The most purely comic of the early historical novels, built on an old collector of inscriptions, coins and family papers whose zeal for the past is turned to account by an impostor and finally defeated by a beggar. Its subject is the social uses of antiquarian knowledge, and its joke is that the past is a property still in dispute. The author held it the most natural of his own tales.
plot_or_argument: Jonathan Oldbuck, the antiquary of Fairport, takes into his house the young stranger Lovel, whose romantic bearing conceals a claim connected with Oldbuck's own family history. The decayed baronet Sir Arthur Wardour, living on credit and on his daughter Isabella's expectations, is seduced by the pretended second-sight of the German trickster Dousterswivel, who is digging for hidden treasure on Oldbuck's land. A French invasion alarm, a runaway elopement, and a death-bed revelation of an abandoned child expose the fraud and settle the rights of the estate. Oldbuck's youthful passion, never followed up, is recovered in the person of Mrs. Stirling, and the beggar Edie Ochiltree, whose evidence has saved him, is provided for in the churchyard monument he had long designed.
narrative_structure: Third-person narration with strongly marked free indirect rendering of the antiquary's own pedantry; a comedy of errors resolved by testimony and revelation; the past is mediated through documents, monuments and tradition rather than narrated directly.
principal_characters: Jonathan Oldbuck; Edie Ochiltree; Sir Arthur Wardour; Isabella Wardour; Lovel; Herman Dousterswivel; Mrs. Stirling; the Rev. Mr. Balwhiddy; the laird of Dumbiedikes
literary_form: Comic novel of manners and character, with antiquarian dissertation and dialect scene; a society comedy of the Borders.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a mixed register of Latin and Scots, burlesque inscription and formal pastiche of the antiquary's own writings.
historical_context: Composed in a few months of extreme financial pressure, and written against the background of the invasion scare of the war years, the collapse of provincial credit, and the thriving trade in forged and romanticised antiquities. Its antiquarian apparatus draws on the same body of Border and monastic materials as the author's editorial work. The volunteer associations and the poor-house pensioners it depicts belong to rural Scotland on the eve of agricultural transformation.
literary_significance: The period's richest novel about the appetite for the past, and the founding text of comic antiquarianism in fiction. It supplies one of the great stock figures of Scottish letters, the collector whose learning is also his meanness. Its treatment of a fake, of testimony and of an inheritance makes it a central text for studies of romantic fraud and of historical evidence.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously as by the Author of Waverley; attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London, 1813, in three volumes, printed by James Ballantyne and Co.; written and published within the same year.

title: Rob Roy
alternative_titles: Rob Roy: A Tale of the Eighteenth Century
description: A tale of the Jacobite rising of 1715 seen from the Lowlands, in which a young Glasgow-Jacobite-Whig merchant's son is drawn into the company of the outlaw chieftain and must repair a commercial fraud committed inside his own family. It is the most autobiographical of the series in its concern with credit, trade and the failure of paper, and the most romantic in its Highland scenery. Its hero-narrator tells his own story in retrospect.
plot_or_argument: Francis Osbaldistone, refused by his father for refusing a counting-house career, is sent to the North to settle affairs with the stubborn tenant Andrew Fairservice, and finds the country in confusion as the Jacobite agents make their preparations. The outlaw Rob Roy, whose wife and children are quartered on the family, dominates the middle of the book; a mysterious player of the violin, in fact a nobleman in disguise, and the beautiful Diana Vernon, betrothed to another, give Francis the passions the plot cannot satisfy. His cousin Rashleigh, who has forged and stolen the title-deeds that ruin the family credit, is defeated at the lodgings in Osbaldistone Hall, the outlaw's justice is procured, the '15 breaks out and is lost, and the narrator is reconciled to trade and to a wife of his own station.
narrative_structure: First-person retrospective narrative by the hero, who reports his education and errors; the political rising is approached obliquely through commerce, hospitality and private fraud; explanatory notes and a later editorial preface record the tradition.
principal_characters: Francis Osbaldistone; Robert 'Rob Roy' MacGregor; Bailie Nicol Jarvey; Diana Vernon; Rashleigh Osbaldistone; Andrew Fairservice; Hildebrand, the disguised fiddler
literary_form: Historical novel and picaresque journey narrative; a commercial and domestic plot set in a time of armed rebellion.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; Scots Lowland speech for Fairservice and the Glasgow bailie, with Highland song and border ballad quoted in the notes.
historical_context: Written in the year of the author's own brush with commercial failure, and much preoccupied with bills, credit and the ruin of a house, which is its real subject. The 1715 rising supplies the political framework, and the Highland-lowland relations of cattle, patronage and law are drawn from the records of the forfeited estates. Its publication at the end of 1817 was timed to the post-war depression that made its anxieties about solvent trading acute.
literary_significance: Created the enduring image of the Highland outlaw as noble bandit and fixed the narrative of Jacobite Scotland for later fiction. Its pairing of a commercial plot with a romantic one makes it the most explicit treatment in the series of money as moral language. It is also the most quoted of the tales for its scenes of hospitality, cattle-feeding and clan mustering.
attribution_notes: Published as by the Author of Waverley; the personal author's name was first prefixed in the 1829-30 collected edition, for which a Memoir and Introduction were written.
bibliographical_notes: First published at the close of 1817 with a title page dated 1818, in three volumes, Edinburgh and London; the change of date on the title page is the reason the work is catalogued now as 1817 and now as 1818.

title: The Tale of Old Mortality
alternative_titles: Tales of My Landlord, First Series
description: The first of the Covenanted series, a novel of the Scottish CAMERONIAN persecutions of the 1670s presented as the transcription of an aged tradition-keeper's papers. Its young hero, drawn equally to the disciplined field-preachers of the south-west and to the disciplined cavalry of the Crown, learns that both causes can consume a private conscience. It is the most unsmiling of the series and the one that most openly interrogates fanaticism and its victims.
plot_or_argument: Henry Morton, the son of a deceased Presbyterian minister and a ward of a Jacobite uncle, is apprenticed to a Covenanting elder and becomes entangled in the armed conventions of the south-west. He loves Edith, the sister of the Cavalier Lord Evandale, and is threatened by John Graham of Claverhouse, the dragoon commander who is at once his patron and his enemy; Morton's capture, sentence and reprieve follow the failure of the rising and the murder of Edith's father. Morton finally takes up arms at Bothwell Brig, is condemned, and is saved by an irregular act of the king's soldier, while Evandale falls in the field on the other side. The aged woman of the title, who keeps the memory of the persecuted, supplies the tale's moral register and its material.
narrative_structure: Framed fiction: the tale is dug out of the papers of an aged traditionary 'Old Mortality' and transcribed by a fictitious idle country gentleman, introduced in a letter from the parish minister; the interior narrative is third-person, with heavy use of sermon, covenant and examination documents.
principal_characters: Henry Morton; Edith Balfour; Lord Evandale; John Graham of Claverhouse; the Old Mortality; Cuddie Headrigg
literary_form: Historical novel of religious war and persecution; a tragedy-plot in prose with a framed antiquarian apparatus.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; Covenanting psalm-tags and field-preaching cadences are quoted and parodied; ballad and psalm verse punctuate the narrative.
historical_context: Drawn from the Cameronian records of the Killing Time after the Restoration, from the conventions and the battles of 1679-80, and from the family traditions of the author's South-Lowland childhood. The introduction records the pleasure a nineteenth-century reader took in religious controversy now dead. Its publication completed the transition from ballad editorship to prose fiction that the war years had made profitable.
literary_significance: The period's greatest novel of religious fanaticism and of the violence done in the name of conscience, and the model for later treatments of Scottish covenanting history. Its frame, in which the past is preserved by an old woman and edited by an idler, is a founding statement of the historical novel's theory of evidence. Its portraits of Claverhouse and of the field-preachers entered the permanent debate about the seventeenth century.
attribution_notes: Published as by the Author of Waverley, the tale being edited by the fictitious 'Landlord'; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London, 1816, in four volumes as the First Series of Tales of My Landlord, printed by James Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Co.

title: The Heart of Midlothian
alternative_titles: Tales of My Landlord, Second Series
The Heart of Midlothian: A Tale
description: The proudest achievement of the series and one of the strongest plots in English fiction: a Scottish plebeian heroine walks to London to save her sister from the gallows. The novel takes the Edinburgh mob, the Tolbooth, the law of infanticide and the royal prerogative of mercy with full seriousness, and its moral argument is carried not by wit but by conscience and a journey. Its title names the Old Tolbooth, 'the Heart of Midlothian'.
plot_or_argument: Effie Deans is condemned to death at Edinburgh for the murder of an infant child, the seducer having concealed his interest and the mother refusing from shame to name him. Her sister Jeanie, holding to the plain rule that a falsehood may not save a life, sets out on foot to London to plead for a reprieve, and on the way is present at the Porteous mob of 1736, when the guard officer who had fired on the crowd is dragged from the Tolbooth and executed on a scaffold reared in the street. Reuben Butler, the presbyterian schoolmaster, follows Jeanie's cause with patience; David Deans, her father, dies of grief and obstinacy. Jeanie's audience with Queen Charlotte, and the intervention of the Duke of Argyll, procure transportation instead of death; the real father, a man of parts and ruin, is exposed, and Jeanie's constancy is rewarded.
narrative_structure: Third-person narrative divided between the Scottish Lowlands and London, with the journey as its spine; the Porteous riot and the dying mother's story are set pieces; the frame is the fictitious landlord who edits the series, and the tale carries a dedicatory preface and notes.
principal_characters: Jeanie Deans; Effie Deans; David Deans; Reuben Butler; Madge Wildfire; George Staunton; the Duke of Argyll; Queen Charlotte; Lady St Ives
literary_form: Historical novel and plebeian romance of the pilgrimage; a legal and domestic tragedy of infanticide and mercy.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; Scots vernacular speech carried at length, with popular song and the burial-service cadence quoted in the scenes of Madge Wildfire.
historical_context: Set in the 1730s, when the Porteous mob and the law of infanticide were live problems of Edinburgh governance, and the Scottish legal system was still negotiating capital punishment for concealed childbirth. The novel's London chapters record the patronage and the royal household of the early Hanoverian court. It was published at the height of the series' commercial power and of the author's own involvement in Edinburgh publishing.
literary_significance: Widely held to be the finest single achievement of the school, and the period's most admired heroine of the people, whose refusal to lie is treated as an act of intellectual as well as moral courage. It fixed the fictional treatment of the Porteous riots and of infanticide law. Its prefatory essay on the composition of the tale is a primary document of the theory of historical fiction.
attribution_notes: Published as by the Author of Waverley in the Tales of My Landlord series; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London, 1818, in four volumes as the Second Series of Tales of My Landlord, printed by James Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Co.

title: The Bride of Lammermoor
alternative_titles: Tales of My Landlord, Third and Fourth Series
description: The most completely tragic of the historical novels, a story of ruined houses and a forced marriage on the Lammermoor coast, told with the series' antiquarian frame but with none of its reconciliation. The feuds of the assembled families are already dying when the plot begins, and the tragedy arises from the collision between an extinguished honour and a working legal ascendency. Its ending is one of the most quoted in Scottish fiction.
plot_or_argument: Edgar, master of Ravenswood, dispossessed by the new law and the new wealth of Sir William Ashton, is warned by the old presbyterian servant of his house not to seek the family of his ruin, and yet loves Ashton's daughter Lucy. Ashton, scheming to secure his office, contracts a marriage between Lucy and the brutal Master of Bucklaw; Ravenswood appears at the contract, is affectedly entertained, and at the Wolf's Head tavern in Edinburgh writes his vow of revenge with a dagger. The nuptials are celebrated, the bride's mind gives way, and Ravenswood, pursued across the Lammermoor sands, perishes in the quicksand at the place long afterwards called the Wolf's Crag, whence neither horse nor rider was ever drawn; Ashton's house falls with him.
narrative_structure: Framed tale in the same editorial apparatus as the series, with the landlord's letter and preface; third-person interior narrative dominated by set scenes of hospitality, contract and pursuit; the concluding disappearance is reported rather than shown.
principal_characters: Edgar, master of Ravenswood; Lucy Ashton; Sir William Ashton; the Master of Bucklaw; Lady Ashton; the Warden of the Three Towers
literary_form: Historical novel and domestic tragedy; gothic romance of the pursued heroine and of the haunted house in the series' frame.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; the high rhetorical cadence of the servant's warnings and of the last scenes, with popular song and prophecy quoted.
historical_context: Set in the reign of Queen Anne at the junction of the Scottish feuding order and the Union's legal government, and drawn from an actual East Lothian family tradition. The novel's atmosphere of extinguished aristocracy reflects the condition of the Border gentry after forfeiture and after the collapse of the Jacobite cause. Its composition followed close on the publication of the preceding series and was partly a reply to criticism of the second.
literary_significance: Provided the archetypal plot of the forced marriage and the lost heiress, and one of the standard scenes of nineteenth-century melodrama and of later opera. It is the fullest example of the school's tragic mode and of its treatment of property, entail and dispossession. Its frame and title-page matter have made it a central text in the editorial history of the series.
attribution_notes: Published as by the Author of Waverley; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London, 1819, in eight volumes as the Third and Fourth Series of Tales of My Landlord, the companion tale in the set being a later legend of the civil war; printed by James Ballantyne and Co.

title: Ivanhoe
description: The romance of twelfth-century England that moved the historical novel away from Scotland and supplied the nineteenth century with its image of medieval chivalry, tournament and Jewry. Its disowned Saxon heir, returned in secret, and its two opposed heroines - the disinherited Rebecca and the Saxon Rowena - carry an argument about tolerance, race and national fusion. The author's dedicated account of the change of subject in the introductory 'Dedicatory Epistle' is itself a famous piece of theory.
plot_or_argument: Wilfred of Ivanhoe, disinherited for following King Richard abroad, appears incognito at the Saxon house of Cedric of Rotherwood, who plans to marry his ward Rowena to a rival claimant of the blood royal. The tourney at Ashby of the Tor, the insults of Prince John's party, and the abduction of the guests at Torquilstone leave the field to outlaws and to the medicine and charity of Rebecca, the Jewess, whom the Templar Brian de Bois-Guilbert pursues to the accusation of trial by combat. Richard returns in disguise, the baronial plot against John is broken, Bois-Guilbert falls dead in the lists, Rebecca is driven out of England by her own people, and Ivanhoe marries Rowena while the disinherited Saxon patrimony is restored.
narrative_structure: Third-person romance in nineteen sections with a 'Dedicatory Epistle' and a 'Letter Prefixed to the Second Edition' on the composition of medieval fiction; the plot is episodic and set-piece driven, with the tournament, the feast and the trial as its pivots.
principal_characters: Wilfred of Ivanhoe; Cedric of Rotherwood; Rowena; Rebecca; Brian de Bois-Guilbert; Front-de-Boeuf; Isaac of York; King Richard I; Prince John; Athelstan; Wamba; Gurth; the Prior Aymer; Ulrica
literary_form: Historical romance and adventure novel of chivalry, with comedy of the lower Saxon characters and a tragedy of the outsider.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; minstrel songs, brindisi and a Jewish hymn are interpolated; the dialogue is keyed to rank, from Norman French-inflected speech to Saxon plainness.
historical_context: Written in the years of the post-Waterloo reaction, when medievalism, national theatre and the question of the civil status of minorities were in the air, and when the author's antiquarian studies had produced a command of the cast, armour and law of the middle ages. The treatment of the Templars and of the Jews draws on a long tradition of English prejudice and on the records of persecution. The book's instant commercial success changed the terms on which historical fiction was commissioned.
literary_significance: Fixed the popular image of medieval England and made the tournament, the castle and the outlaw band the standard equipment of romance; it also made the suffering Jewess one of the century's most discussed fictional creations. Its explicit theory of how a modern writer may fabricate a past has been continuously cited. Its influence on the medieval revival, in fiction, stage design and costume, is extensive.
attribution_notes: Published as by the Author of Waverley; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London in three volumes with a title page dated 1820, issued at the close of 1819 by Archibald Constable and Co. with Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme and Brown; the copyright brought one of the largest sums then paid for a novel.

title: The Lay of the Last Minstrel
alternative_titles: The Lay of the Last Minstrel: A Poem
description: The poem that created the national metrical romance of the Borders, framed as the song of the last of the itinerant minstrels, who sings for hospitality at the house of Branksome and tells of a feud, a love and a raised corpse of the generation before the Union. Its explanatory notes, collected border tradition and deliberate archaism made it the first full-scale application of antiquarian method to original narrative verse. Its success turned a collector of ballads into a poet.
plot_or_argument: The aged minstrel, taken in at the castle, sings of the baron of Branksome, whose death in the burial vault is foretold, and of the love of his daughter Margaret for the English captive Henry, which the feud of the houses of Branksome and Cragside forbids. The champion Deloraine, under bond not to shed Christian blood, is sent to raise the dead from the vault of Melrose by the help of the monk and the goblin page Gilpin Horner, who is begotten and bred of conjuring. The spirit's warning, the page's fatal errand and the marriage that ends the quarrel close the lay; the minstrel's own age and the passing of his order frame the whole.
narrative_structure: Six cantos with an 'Introductory Epistle' in which the author accounts for the measure and design; the framing scene of the aged singer gives the poem its meditative onsets and closings, and each canto contains songs and ballad interpolations.
principal_characters: The last minstrel; Margaret of Branksome; Henry the English captive; Deloraine, the outlaw champion; Gilpin Horner, the goblin page; the monk of Melrose
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; a border antiquarian poem with framing ballad-singer and learned notes.
meter_and_prosody: Stanzas of iambic tetrameter in the mixed romantic measure the author took from the old border poets, varied by ballad stanzas and lyric songs.
historical_context: Composed in the years when the author was editing the border minstrelsy and when the claims of national and popular poetry were being argued in the reviews; the poem's sixteenth-century setting looks back to the last generation of the free border. Its publication, early in 1805, was timed to a revived demand for romance while the war with France made the past feel lost. Its sale in the first three years established the commercial model for the long poem.
literary_significance: Opened the vogue for the metrical romance that dominated narrative poetry for two decades, and set the standard for the use of border ballad and antiquarian note inside original verse. Its framing device of the last of a dying order supplied the century's most durable image of oral tradition extinguished. The poem's success created the public for which the prose romances were afterwards written.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's own name; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published January 1805, London, for Longman, Hurst, Rees and Orme, and Edinburgh, for Archibald Constable and Co., printed by James Ballantyne and Co.; six editions appeared within three years.

title: Marmion
alternative_titles: Marmion: A Tale of Flodden Field
description: The second and greater metrical romance, a tale of the Scottish border on the eve of Flodden in which a subtle and unscrupulous courtier forges a false appeal of treason against the lover of the woman he desires. Its argument is carried by a villain of the law rather than by a hero, and its prefaced epistle to a friend on the difference between prose romance and metrical romance is one of the period's key statements of theory. The battle, the doom and the convent scenes gave the poem its immense popularity.
plot_or_argument: Marmion, lord of Fontenelle and captain of Norham, loves the Lady Clara de Clare, who is betrothed to Sir Ralph de Wilton; to clear the way he procures a counterfeit appeal of treason against Wilton, and the trial at the bar of the king's bench is fought out with perjured evidence. Clara and her sister Constance, who has been wronged by Marmion and kept in a convent, die of the ruin he brings on them; Wilton escapes to the north. Marmion, abandoned by every claim he had made, rides against Scotland, and at Flodden, unhorsed and desperate, challenges Wilton alone; he dies of his wounds, having first confessed his fraud, while the Scottish king and his host are cut up in the field.
narrative_structure: Six cantos preceded by an 'Epistle to William Erskine' on the writing of romance and interspersed with ballad, song and the independent 'Death of Constance' episode; the frame loosens as the poem moves from narrative to set piece.
principal_characters: Marmion; Clara de Clare; Sir Ralph de Wilton; Constance de Beverley; James IV of Scotland
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse, combining historical battle poem, legal thriller and convent gothic.
meter_and_prosody: Principally iambic tetrameter couplets in the short 'hitching' measure of the earlier poem, with ballad stanzas, hymn and lyric interpolation.
historical_context: Written between the war with France and the renewal of national anxiety about invasion, and built on the records of the 1513 campaign and on the antiquarian collections of the border. Its depiction of early Tudor law, of the appeal of treason and of the bar reflects the author's own professional familiarity with the courts of Edinburgh. The poem's dedication and epistles were shaped by the contemporary review debate over romance and probability.
literary_significance: Carried the metrical romance to its highest commercial pitch and supplied the century's best-known verses on battle and on national feeling. Its prefaced essay on romance, probability and the machinery of verse was much imitated and much discussed. The figure of the accomplished, amoral courtier gave the school of romantic narrative one of its permanent villains.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's own name; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London, 1808, in two volumes, printed by James Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Co. and for Longman, Hurst, Rees and Orme; several editions followed within the year.

title: The Lady of the Lake
alternative_titles: The Lady of the Lake: A Poem
description: The third and most popular of the metrical romances, a Highland tale of a royal progress in disguise, a banished lord and a maiden reared in the wilds of the Trossachs. Its rapid octosyllabic movement, its lake, cave and gathering-of-the-clans set pieces, and its elaborate notes on Highland custom made it the best-selling narrative poem of its generation. It was advertised as the work that would decide whether the author's verse should continue.
plot_or_argument: King James the Fifth, touring the south of the Highlands in the summer under the borrowed name of Fitz-James, loses his attendance in a long chase and is guided by a mountaineer to the caves and island recesses of the lake country, where he is harboured by an aged hermit and by the outlawed Douglas, the last of his line. There he sees Ellen, Douglas's daughter, reared among the wilds, whom the young minstrel Malcolm Graeme loves and whom the chieftain Roderick Dhu of Clan Alpine would win. Roderick, at feud with Douglas and slighted in his suit, gathers his clan and joins the enemies of the crown; the king's stranger is drawn into the pursuit, and an illegal arrow almost ends his part. The quarrel is brought to judgement at Stirling, where a champion in unknown arms fights before the king's court for the attainted lord; the royal secret is disclosed, honours are distributed, Roderick dies of his wounds, and Ellen is married to the lover of her youth.
narrative_structure: Six cantos of continuous romance narrative with a lyrical opening invocation and a closing epistle to a noble patron, supported by copious antiquarian notes on Highland customs; the set pieces - the boat-song on the lake, the gathering of the clan, the cave, the combat at Stirling - carry the structure.
principal_characters: King James the Fifth; Ellen, the Lady of the Lake; Douglas, the banished lord; Roderick Dhu, chief of Clan Alpine; Malcolm Graeme; the hermit of St. Bride
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; Highland romance with court intrigue and a disguised monarch plot.
meter_and_prosody: Iambic tetrameter couplets in the easy short measure already used in the earlier romances, with ballad stanzas, hymns, a boat-song and an epithalamium interpolated.
historical_context: Published in the year of Napoleon's ascendancy in Europe, when the demand for national romance was at its height and when Highland costume and clan history were being simultaneously documented and romanticised. The author's notes draw on the statistical and antiquarian survey of Scotland then in progress. Its dedication and its epistles engage directly with the review controversy about the value of romantic poetry.
literary_significance: The most widely sold and most translated British narrative poem of the second decade of the century, and the chief conduit through which Highland Scotland entered the popular imagination of the nineteenth century. Its scenery, its hilloa gathering and its lake scene became standard equipment for later verse, painting and stage spectacle. Its success hastened the author's decision to abandon verse for prose fiction.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's own name; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London, 1810, printed by James Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Co. and for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme and Brown; many editions and translations followed within the decade.

title: Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border
alternative_titles: Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, in Three Volumes
description: The great editorial work that supplied the raw material and the theory for the border romances: traditional ballads of the South, gathered from recitation and from printed and manuscript copies, with an introduction historical and traditional, explanatory notes, and essays on chivalry and on romantic poetry. It preserves 'Sir Patrick Spens', 'Thomas the Rhymer', 'The Battle of Otterbourne' and a large body of Border narrative verse, and it prints in its later volumes imitations and pieces composed by the editor himself. Its methods of conjectural restoration and of making up defective copies became a central case in the history of ballad editing.
plot_or_argument: The collection is organised historically rather than narratively: a preliminary account of the border minstrels and of the conditions of their production; then the ballads of real or alleged history, arranged in chronological order with their traditions, from the fourteenth century to the Union; then the romantic and fantastical tales of the same region; and, in the volumes of imitations, pieces written in the ancient manner. The notes record authorities, variants and the circumstances of recitation, and the dissolving legend of Robin Hood receives an early essay.
narrative_structure: Editorial anthology: framing dissertation, texts in sequence, and scholarly commentary; no single plot. Individual ballads supply their own narrative structures, from the abrupt scene-ballad to the metrical chronicle and the lyrical lament.
literary_form: Anthology, reliques and editorial collection of popular balladry, with attached critical dissertation; the verse proper belongs to lyrical ballad and popular stanza.
meter_and_prosody: The ballad stanzas of the Scottish and Border popular tradition (common-measure and 'Marginal' four-line stanzas, often with refrain), with alliterative and Chronicle-verse residues; the editor's own imitations follow the same stanzas.
historical_context: Gathered in the 1790s from oral reciters, from the manuscript collections of the Borders and from the printed sheets, at the moment when the old border recitation was ceasing and when the great mid-century anthologies of ancient national verse had made balladry a national property. Its publication coincided with the war years' appetite for native antiquity. The editor was a lawyer and an antiquary, and the collection's standards of evidence are those of the Scottish historical profession of the 1790s.
literary_significance: The foundation of modern Scottish ballad studies and a decisive model for the scholarly editing of popular verse; it also furnished plots, characters and phrases for the metrical romances and for the historical novels that followed. Its editorial licence - conjecture, restoration and interpolation - provoked the longest controversy in ballad scholarship. Its historical introduction remains a classic account of the social conditions of oral poetry.
attribution_notes: The editor's own imitations and pieces are distinguished in the collection from the traditional texts; no dispute over the editorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh, 1802, in two volumes, printed by James Ballantyne and Co.; a third volume of modern imitations appeared in 1803, and a second edition in four volumes, with the added essays, in 1806; a third edition with a new historical introduction appeared in 1833.

title: Castle Rackrent
description: The first Irish national novel and one of the earliest great uses of an unreliable vernacular narrator: the hereditary steward of a long-descended family tells, with unshakable loyalty, the history of the four or five squires who wasted his master's estate. It is a comic chronicle of absenteeism, gaming, lawyers, electioneering and imprudent improvement, closing on the Act of Union. Its prefatory memoir and its explanatory glossary of Hibernian terms, both supplied by an editor, place the tale at a deliberate historical distance from its readers.
plot_or_argument: Thady Quirk, born on the estate and servant to four generations, reports the successive squires: the easy first squire, who quarrelled with his brother and died; the next, whose extravagance and whose family's intrigue over an heiress and an elopement brought in lawyers; the lawyer squire, a devout bigot who worried his tenants with process; the dissolute absentee; and finally the improving and popular last squire, whose well-meant schemes of cultivation, his marriage to an Englishwoman, and the machinations of Thady's own son about the deeds, consume the property. The family's representative votes for Union, the estate passes out of the name, and the steward dies unprosperous but content.
narrative_structure: First-person memoir by the steward, edited and annotated by a scholarly 'Editor' who supplies a family memoir before and a note after the narrative; chronological by squire, with dialect glosses and documentary intrusions (leases, bills, an oath).
principal_characters: Thady Quirk, the steward-narrator; the successive squires of Castle Rackrent, from the first squire to the improving last; Constantia, an injured heiress of the family; Kit Corry, her eloping lover; Myrtle, the English wife of the last squire; the Editor of the memoir
literary_form: Comic chronicle-novel and character tale; the first of the national tales, an estate history told in servant's Hibernian-English.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a sustained Irish vernacular voice, with proverb, biblical tag and law-phrase, and an explanatory glossary of Hibernian-English.
historical_context: Written in the years after the 1798 rising and published in the year of the Act of Union, its subject is the Irish Ascendancy's management of land, law and loyalty. The tale's distance from contemporary politics is itself political: it treats the misgovernment of Ireland as a social comedy of manners and tenures. Its authorship grew out of household education and of the publisher's demand for improvement literature, and it was read as an explanation of the Union to an English public.
literary_significance: Founded the national tale and the Big House novel, and set the pattern of the loyal partisan narrator whose testimony the reader must reconstruct. It is the earliest extended use of Irish vernacular speech as the governing medium of an English novel, and a standard document for the history of the absentee estate. Its framing apparatus made it a model for the edited and annotated tale.
attribution_notes: The first edition carried the attribution to the author of an earlier pedagogical work rather than a name; authorship has never been in doubt.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1800, in three volumes; a second edition in the same year added the Editor's Memoir and Glossary. The manuscript of the tale survives in family papers.

title: Popular Tales
description: A three-volume collection of short tales for young readers and their families, the most internationally influential children's and domestic fiction of its decade. It mixes Irish, English and colonial settings, and turns the practical problems of temper, vanity, falsehood and fortune into close-analysed children's actions. Its title marks a deliberate theory of popularity: instruction designed to be read for pleasure.
plot_or_argument: The collection proceeds by separate tales rather than a continuous plot: a child's stubbornness and its correction; a boy's vanity about his birth and a father's silence; a slave's return of a stolen estate in a West Indian insurrection; the deceptions of a child who cannot tell a lie from a fiction; and tales of trade, of Irish tenantry and of school emulation. Each closes with a plainly stated moral consequence rather than with marriage or inheritance.
narrative_structure: Discrete short tales in three volumes, each with a self-contained crisis and an explicit moral resolution; a plain, explanatory narration with frequent dialogue and written documents such as letters and accounts.
literary_form: Juvenile and domestic tale collection; character-writing and moral experiment in short prose fiction.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; plain conversational style with deliberately differentiated speech for children and for Irish and colonial characters.
historical_context: Produced in a household devoted to educational experiment and to the publishing of children's books, and aimed at the expanding middle-class market for family reading after the pedagogical controversies of the 1790s. Its West Indian tale engages directly with the plantation insurrection of 1760 and with contemporary abolitionist argument. Its Irish tales assume the post-Union question of how the tenant might be represented to an English reader.
literary_significance: Set the standard for the analysed juvenile action in English fiction and shaped the pedagogical novel of the nineteenth century; it was translated widely and praised by contemporary critics and reviewers of the higher literature. Its handling of colonial and Irish material makes it a focal text for the study of the period's domestic ideology. Its editorial practice - prefacing tales with arguments on their use - is a document of period literary theory.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's own name; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1804, in three volumes; issued with plates and rapidly reprinted; several tales had circulated in manuscript and in an earlier educational volume.

title: Ennui
description: The most searching of the Irish tales of the post-Union decade, a story of an English-raised young nobleman whose listlessness is broken by the discovery that his Irish tenancy and his very title rest on a suppressed claim. It is a tale of identity, of the consequences of concealed evidence, and of what the writer calls ennui as a social as well as a moral disease. Its framing documents - letters and a deposition - make it a central instance of the period's edited Irish fiction.
plot_or_argument: The hero, a young man of wealth and no occupation, wastes his time in England among friends who flatter him, and returns to his Irish estate where the claims of an old dependant family begin to interrupt his possessions. An attached narrative, put in the mouth of a half-witted Irish retainer whose shrewdness is the tale's engine, discloses the history of the exchanged child and of the evidence that would ruin him. The woman of the family who has loved him dies; his rival in claim recovers his own place; and the reformed hero, stripped of his assumed name, must build a life out of the loss. The tale ends in a marriage and in a hard-won purpose.
narrative_structure: Framed and documentary: a main third-person narrative interrupted by an embedded Irish oral narration and by letters and papers; the embedded teller's voice carries the revelation that changes the plot.
principal_characters: The young English-raised nobleman of the title; the Irish dependant whose claim displaces him; the faithful half-witted retainer who tells the family history; the Irish woman whose fate his idleness touches
literary_form: National tale and domestic romance; a frame narrative of the post-Union Irish estate novel.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; alternation of polite English narration with Hibernian-English oral storytelling.
historical_context: Written in the years after the Union, when the settlement of the Irish Ascendancy's estates, the question of concealed title, and the education of a landlord class were pressing public matters. Its diagnosis of ennui is a diagnosis of a class with property and no function. The author's household background in law, estate management and educational writing supplies the tale's technical knowledge of evidence and claim.
literary_significance: One of the most subtle fictional analyses of Anglo-Irish property and identity before the famine novel, and a key document of the national tale after the first and best-known example of the form. Its use of an Irish oral narrator inside an English frame has been much studied. It supplies the period's fullest fictional account of boredom as a social condition.
attribution_notes: First published under a designation referring to an earlier tale rather than under the author's name; authorship undisputed. Certain details of the frame and of the naming of the principal characters are not asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1809 as a separate tale; it was soon collected with the author's other Irish fiction. The date of the first impression is not disputed; the volume format of the first issue is not stated here.

title: Letters for Literary Ladies
description: An early polemical work in the form of letters addressed to women readers, arguing that the cultivation of the understanding is the duty and the happiness of their sex, and that the fashionable restrictions on female study rest on authority rather than on reason. It replies directly to the influential prescription of the period that women should be amused rather than instructed. The book is also a piece of family literary history, since one of its letters is addressed to a young woman of the household for whom the writer's educational books had been made.
plot_or_argument: The letters urge that women may read history, philosophy and the sciences without loss of tenderness or of domestic virtue; they argue that the pleasures of the imagination are a support in adversity and that an uncultivated mind makes an unequal marriage. They concede the danger of pedantry and of public display, and insist that the improvement of the female understanding will improve the education of children and the morals of the family. The argument is conducted through example, quotation and courteous concession rather than through declaration.
narrative_structure: Epistolary argument in two volumes, addressed to named private correspondents; no plot, and the sequence is one of theme rather than event.
literary_form: Conduct, education and domestic prose in epistolary form; a polemic and open letter addressed to a reading public.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a light, ironical, conversational period style with frequent quotation.
historical_context: Written in the aftermath of the 1790s debate about female education, on which the revolutionary controversy had made the instruction of women a political question as well as a domestic one. It belongs to the household educational enterprise of its author, whose writing was first done for the instruction of younger members of her family. Its publication preceded by five years the national tale that made her name, and it shows her first use of the printed public.
literary_significance: An important document of the transition from conduct literature to the argument for women's intellectual cultivation at the end of the eighteenth century. It supplies evidence of how a woman writer entered the print public sphere by way of the familiar letter. Its arguments were to be reworked, without polemic, in the fictional illustrations of the tales.
attribution_notes: The first edition did not print the author's name; her authorship was established immediately within the family and publishing circle and is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1795, in two volumes, in a familiar-letter format; reprinted in a single volume in 1796 with the writer's name prefixed.

title: Things as They Are; or, The Adventures of Caleb Williams
description: The founding novel of philosophical anarchy and of the pursuit plot, written to dramatise the argument that private virtue is destroyed by law, rank and the arbitrary power of a benefactor. Its hero, a curious clerk who forces out of his patron the secret of an old murder, becomes the victim of an inexorable persecution that carries him from a country house to a London prison. The novel's machinery of spies, forgery, false arrest and flight supplied the gothic and sensation plotting of the next half-century.
plot_or_argument: Caleb Williams, the son of an old dependant of the country gentleman Falkland, is educated, made secretary and admired, and by an unlucky question extracts from his benefactor the confession that years before he killed a low and malignant rival in the fight over an estate.
