Falkland's pride turns to alarm and then to systematic persecution: Caleb is dismissed, falsely suspected of theft, pursued through the country and driven to London, where, poor and unknown, he is befriended by an alderman and by a man of ruined reputation, and is at last trapped by an artifice of friendship into a spunging-house and a marshal's custody. Escape, disguise and a project of revenge put weapons in his hands; he returns to England, extorts from Falkland a public confession, and stands by while his persecutor is prosecuted, convicted and sent into exile, where he dies. Caleb, the victor, has spent his patron's fortune and ruined his own prospects, and the tale closes with the writing of his confession.
narrative_structure: First-person confession written by the hero and addressed to the public; three volumes of continuous pursuit, with an inserted narrative told by another sufferer; a conclusion that reports the deaths of both principals.
principal_characters: Caleb Williams; Falkland, the patron who becomes his persecutor; Mr. Bailey, the London alderman who befriends him; Julian, the friend who is ruined by his kindness to the hero
literary_form: Philosophical and anarchist fiction; picaresque pursuit novel and domestic gothic of lawless power.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; rapid first-person argumentative narrative with long analytical passages and colloquial dialogue of clubs, prisons and the road.
historical_context: Written in the train of a systematic treatise on justice published the year before, and in the atmosphere of the 1790s controversies over law, aristocratic privilege and the efficacy of punishment. Its legal machinery reflects the actual procedures of civil arrest, spunging-houses and criminal trial at the close of the century. Its publication was followed by denunciation in the ministerial press as a school of Jacobinism, and a table of the contents of the argument was prefixed to the first edition.
literary_significance: The most influential English novel of persecution and of the psychology of a tyrant and his victim, and the work that gave the pursued-hero plot its secular, legal form. Its treatment of class power, of the spectacle of punishment and of the failure of revenge makes it a founding text of political fiction. Later gothic, sensation and detective fiction inherited its apparatus of spies, forgeries and prisons.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. Early copies are dated 1793 or 1794 according to the issue of the last volume.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1794, in three volumes, printed for G. G. and J. Robinson; reprinted in the collected editions of the author's tales, the last of which restored readings suppressed in the middle editions.

title: St. Leon
alternative_titles: St. Leon: A Tale of the Sixteenth Century
description: A tale of the secret of gold, in which an unlucky nobleman receives from a wandering Hebrew the alchemical formula for the philosopher's stone and the elixir of life, and finds that boundless wealth destroys every human tie. It applies the earlier novel's analysis of persecution to a new subject: the moral consequences of economic power without social obligation. Its framing as a sixteenth-century narrative gave the alchemical and wanderer traditions a modern philosophical use.
plot_or_argument: Raymond, count of St. Leon, ruined by his father's losses and by a quarrel with the house of his bride, is thrown upon the road in Germany with his wife and infant son. In a solitary retreat he meets the undying wanderer, who purchases his silence with the secret of transmutation and of the elixir; the gift makes him rich, and wealth makes him a stranger to his family, an object of suspicion to the state and at last a hunted man. Pursued by the agents of a rival claimant and by the creditors of a fabricated prosperity, he assumes other names, loses his son's confidence and his wife's trust, and at length flies to America with a fortune that can buy no repose. The narrative closes on the exhaustion of a man who has outlived every motive by which men are held together.
narrative_structure: First-person confession from a manuscript found and published by an editor; continuous autobiographical narrative with embedded letters and an account of the wanderer's own history.
principal_characters: Raymond, count of St. Leon; the undying wanderer who reveals the secret of gold; his wife; his son; the agents who pursue him
literary_form: Philosophical tale and alchemical romance; a gothic-tinged analysis of wealth in the form of a confessional autobiography.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a measured, argumentative first-person style in which the marvellous is related in the tones of evidence.
historical_context: Written in the years of the author's own financial desperation and of furious controversy over property, credit and the paper economy. The legends of the Wandering Jew and of the philosopher's stone supplied a familiar machinery which the novel turns to the analysis of money. Its publication coincided with the renewal of the same radical publishing interest that had issued the earlier tales.
literary_significance: The most complete application of eighteenth-century philosophical fiction to the problem of wealth, and an important source for the nineteenth-century novel of the man who can buy anything. It preserved and reinterpreted the alchemical and wanderer legends for a rational age. Its influence on later treatments of immortality, of the isolated benefactor and of domestic ruin is considerable.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1799, in three volumes, printed for G. G. and J. Robinson; reissued in the collected editions of the tales of the early nineteenth century.

title: Mandeville
description: The last of the great philosophical tales and the most explicitly historical, a narrative of the Wars of the Roses written by a Lancashire gentleman at the close of the Elizabethan age. Its subject is enthusiasm - religious, romantic and political - and its argument, delivered at length in the narrator's reflections, is that the human understanding is corrupted by the temper of the age in which it is trained. The book also conducts a late quarrel: its author had long been accused of impiety, and the tale defends the imaginative temper while satirising its excesses.
plot_or_argument: Charles Mandeville, of a family impoverished by the part its father took in the rival cause, is bound as page to a noble household, is driven by a youthful attachment into the opposing camp, and is thrown by chance into the society of a band of outlaws and of a wandering scholar of mock philosophy. He passes through the great events of the period, is captured, escapes, and returns to a love he has been taught to distrust. The framing narrator, old and solitary under Elizabeth, revises his judgments on fortune, on religious zeal and on the claims of romance, and ends with a defence of enthusiasm of the mind against the merely cautious understanding.
narrative_structure: Autobiographical manuscript of an old man, written in the later sixteenth century about the earlier fifteenth, with long reflective digressions; recollection interrupted by direct address and by quoted documents.
principal_characters: Mandeville, the narrating Lancashire gentleman; the household to which he is a dependant; the outlaw company; the wandering scholar he befriends
literary_form: Historical novel and philosophical autobiography; a tale of the civil wars with a framing essay on enthusiasm.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; an archaising, sententious periodic style with deliberate antiquarian colouring.
historical_context: Composed during the last war with France and published at the moment when romance and history were being made into a national industry; its treatment of civil war, superstition and fanaticism answers both the historical romances of the day and the long dispute about enthusiasm in the author's earlier essays. Its Elizabethan framing allows a double historical perspective on the fifteenth century. The novel sold poorly and marks the end of its author's career as a fiction-writer.
literary_significance: The most sustained attempt of the philosophical school to fuse history, romance and argument in a single narrative, and an important document of the late debate over enthusiasm and the imagination. Its historical machinery belongs to the same current of antiquarian research that produced the rival school of romance. It is now chiefly studied as the term of an experiment begun a quarter of a century before.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1817, in three volumes; reprinted in the collected tales of the early 1830s with prefatory matter by the author.

title: A Vindication of the Rights of Men
description: The earliest and one of the most energetic replies to a celebrated conservative meditation on the French Revolution, written in a matter of weeks and issued anonymously as a letter to the author of the Reflections. It argues that the rights of men are not derived from prescription, rank or inherited opinion, and that a scheme of society built on pomp and subordination is a betrayal of reason and of the poor. The pamphlet made its writer a recognised polemicist and founded the vocabulary of her later work.
plot_or_argument: The letter attacks the description of chivalry, of a natural aristocracy of rank and of the sanctified majesty of kings as the sources of social order, and insists that virtue belongs to individuals and not to titles. It contrasts the sympathy which a sentimental attachment to the past excites with the real suffering of living men, and holds that taste and feeling may not be pleaded against justice. It defends the rights of conscience and of enquiry, ridicules the argument from prescription, and concludes that a reform of the state grounded in reason and in the duty of benevolence is the only honourable answer to the present crisis.
narrative_structure: Continuous epistolary polemic addressed to a named opponent; argument by extract and refutation, with long rhetorical passages on sympathy, rank and opulence; a second edition added postscripts answering the replies.
literary_form: Polemic, pamphlet and open letter; political and revolutionary argument in prose.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a high rhetorical style of quotation, apostrophe and rapid refutation.
historical_context: Written within months of the publication of the most influential attack on the recent revolution, at the opening of the Revolution Controversy, when a large pamphlet literature on prescription, rights and the condition of the poor appeared monthly. Its publisher was the centre of the dissenting and radical book trade. The pamphlet's success established the terms on which the rights of men and of women would afterwards be argued together.
literary_significance: The first important challenge by a woman writer to the rhetoric of prescriptive conservatism, and the opening document of a career that would connect the question of rights with the condition of women. Its analysis of sentiment as a political instrument anticipated much later argument. It stands as a primary text of the 1790s debate on revolution, rank and benevolence.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously in 1790; attribution established by contemporary correspondence and by the publisher's records, and not in dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, December 1790, as a pamphlet; a second edition with postscripts followed in 1791.

title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
alternative_titles: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: with Strictures on Political and Moral Subjects
description: The founding text of modern argument for women's rational education: a vindication contending that female weakness is the artifact of false systems of education and of the cult of sensibility, and that women must be made reasonable to become companions, citizens and mothers. It is addressed to a legislator of a neighbouring republic and rests on the premise that rights follow from the capacity to reason. Its mixture of system, satire and complaint made it at once a philosophical treatise and a scandal.
plot_or_argument: The work first lays down the principle that the understanding of women, like that of men, must be cultivated if virtue is to exist, then surveys the false education which makes them anxious for beauty and expedient for marriage. It examines the literature and the conduct books that form the female mind, attacks the doctrine of sexual refinement, and argues for a common standard of rational cultivation, for the occupations open to women and for a new seriousness in female friendship and duty. It closes with strictures on the regulations of health, of motherhood and of the character which a rational education might produce, and with an appeal to women themselves to claim the improvement of their faculties.
narrative_structure: Thirteen chapters of continuous argument with embedded strictures on particular authors and institutions; a dedication to a statesman frames the work; the method alternates between systematic proposition, historical survey and invective.
literary_form: Philosophical treatise and polemic in the form of a vindication; conduct and educational prose transformed into an argument for civic rights.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; an urgent, abstract yet passionate style with long periods, direct address and rhetorical question.
historical_context: Written in the middle of the 1790s controversy over education, gender and the rights of man, after the author's first pamphlet on the same subject and during her work as a reviewer for the radical book trade. Its arguments answer the most widely read prescription for female accomplishment, and its examples come from the conduct literature, schools and marriage law of the period. Its reception was immediate, hostile and extensive.
literary_significance: The central text of the literature on women's rational and civic capacity, and the work from which most later argument about education, dependence and citizenship derived. It created a critical vocabulary for the analysis of femininity as production rather than nature. Its recovery in the late twentieth century made it canonical in literary as well as in political history.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name and with a reference to her earlier work; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1792, in one volume, by the bookseller who had issued her earlier pamphlet; a second edition appeared within the year, and translations followed in the same decade.

title: Letters Written in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark
alternative_titles: Letters Written during a Short Residence in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark
description: A book of travel letters written on a northern tour in the summer and autumn of 1795 and revised for the press the following year; it is at once a scenic account of Sweden and Norway, a survey of their commerce, manners and government, and a journal of private grief. The letters are addressed to the partner whose commercial interests the journey was meant to recover, and are signed with a single initial. Its mixture of picturesque observation, political economy and lament makes it the most subtle of the period's travel narratives.
plot_or_argument: The letters follow a ship and a coach from London through Elsinore, Gothenburg and the Swedish coast, up the Norwegian rivers and to the cascade of Rjukanfoss and Telemark, and then through Denmark and back. Along the road the writer records the faces of the poor, the condition of women, the management of forests and mines, the laws of Sweden, the manners of the Norwegian peasants and the scenery of rock and waterfall, and repeatedly tests the theories of the sublime and of taste against what she has seen. Interwoven with this is the account of a failed negotiation, of a deserted woman's tenderness and of thoughts of death that the northern landscape seems to invite and then to dispel. The closing letters turn from the individual complaint to a project of moral and political improvement for the nations of the north.
narrative_structure: Twenty-five familiar letters in chronological order of travel, shifting between report, essay and confession; the second-person addressee gives the sequence its emotional continuity, while the description and the disquisition carry its argument.
literary_form: Travel letters and familiar essay in epistolary form; topographical and political observation fused with a diary of feeling.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; an elastic, exclamatory style that moves from precise observation to apostrophe, with quoted verse and song fragments.
historical_context: Written in the aftermath of the revolutionary decade, when travel in the north had become an object of commercial and diplomatic interest and when the picturesque was the dominant vocabulary of landscape description. Its economic observations belong to the debate about national prosperity opened by the new political economy. The tour was undertaken to retrieve a partner's failing speculation in Scandinavian trade, and the book's private address reflects that entanglement.
literary_significance: The most admired prose narrative of its author's later work and a central text of Romantic travel writing; it influenced the northern travelogue and the lyric meditation on landscape for a century. Its analysis of the sublime from a woman's travelling consciousness is a much-studied contribution to the period's aesthetic debate. It is also a primary document of the history of feeling, commerce and gender in the 1790s.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1796, in one volume, by the bookseller of her earlier works; drawn from letters written on the 1795 tour and revised for the press; a posthumous collected edition gathered the travel writings in 1798.

title: An Historical and Moral View of the Origin and Progress of the French Revolution
alternative_titles: An Historical and Moral View of the Origin and Progress of the French Revolution; and the Effect It Has Produced in Europe
description: A philosophical history of the Revolution written partly on the scene itself, which treats the French event as the symptom of a long civilisation and asks what its moral effects have been on Europe. It defends the original causes of the Revolution while condemning the violence that followed, and explains both by the corrupt institutions of the old regime and by the temper of a people unprepared for free inquiry. It is the period's clearest attempt to hold revolutionary hope and revolutionary disappointment in a single argument.
plot_or_argument: The work first states the general causes: the accumulated superstition, the inequality of ranks, the vices of an exhausted monarchy and the progress of letters that had prepared the crisis. It then traces the opening acts of the Revolution, the conduct of the assemblies, the errors of the court and the character of the parties, with sustained attention to the motives of individuals. The later chapters examine the effects produced in Europe, the spirit of party, the tendency of the violence to discredit the cause, and the prospects of a slower moral improvement that may yet fulfil the expectations the Revolution defeated. The conclusion is cautious: the principles are vindicated, the event is mourned.
narrative_structure: Systematic historical essay in preface and numbered sections, moving from general causes to narrative sequence to moral reflection; no continuous chronicle but an argumentative arrangement of events.
literary_form: Philosophical and national history; political treatise and moral essay on a contemporary event.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a cool analytical style enlivened by rapid characterisation and by rhetorical generalisation.
historical_context: Composed during the author's residence in Paris and on the return journey in 1792-93, through the trial of the king, the wars and the Terror, and published after the executions had made optimism difficult to defend. It belongs to the literature of the revolutionary exile and of the British debate over sympathy with France. Its argument answers both the conservative prediction of ruin and the radical expectation of regeneration.
literary_significance: A key document of the transatlantic Revolution Controversy and one of the earliest attempts to write the history of a living revolution as moral philosophy. It supplies the period's most articulate statement of disappointed yet unretracted revolutionary hope. Its reading of enthusiasm, prejudice and national character links it to the philosophical history of the Scottish schools.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1794, in two volumes, by the bookseller of her polemic and educational writings; parts of the argument were drafted in France in 1792-93.

title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
description: The tale of a modern Prometheus: a Genevan student who learns to kindle animation in dead matter, and the reasoning creature his labour brings into being. It is written as a series of confessions nested inside the letters of an Arctic navigator, and its argument concerns the duties of a maker to his work, the miseries of an unprotected intelligence, and the revenge of knowledge pursued without sympathy. Its 1831 revision, prefixed by a new account of its composition, is the text most often read.
plot_or_argument: Robert Walton, wintering in the northern ocean, takes aboard a half-dead traveller who tells his history: Victor Frankenstein, bred in prosperity, masters natural philosophy, assembles a being from materials and, horrified at his own success, abandons it. The creature, instructed by observation and by a lost volume of philosophy, demands companions; refused, it murders Victor's brother, allows an innocent servant to be executed for the deed, destroys the mate intended for it, and kills Victor's bride on his wedding night. Victor pursues his maker's enemy to the north, is there lost in the ice, and dies on board the navigator's ship, having warned him from the same ambition. The creature appears at the bedside and vows to consume itself in the frozen ocean.
narrative_structure: Triple-frame narration: the letters of the Arctic captain enclose the traveller's first-person confession, which in turn encloses the creature's own long defence; the three accounts contradict and confirm each other without a final arbitrating voice.
principal_characters: Victor Frankenstein; the creature he makes; Robert Walton, the Arctic captain; Elizabeth Lavenza; Henry Clerval; Alphonse Frankenstein; Caroline Beaufort; William; Justine Moritz
literary_form: Gothic novel and romance of terror with a philosophical tale of creation inside an Arctic narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; elevated eighteenth-century rhetorical narration, with the creature's set speeches in a more Latinate and self-taught idiom.
historical_context: Conceived in the summer of 1816, the year without a summer, among a party of exiles and experimenters on the lake of Geneva, out of a wager to produce tales of the supernatural, and written out after the return to England. Its science reflects the current interest in galvanism and in the chemistry of life, and its frame draws on the published narratives of polar voyages. The 1831 revision was made in response to a demand for a standard collected text and quietly altered the account of its own origin.
literary_significance: The most durable myth of modern culture, supplying the vocabulary in which the responsibilities of the scientist, the grievances of the made and the terrors of solitary ambition are discussed. It transformed the gothic tale of terror into a philosophical narrative with two contested narrators, and founded a line of fiction and stage spectacle that continues. Its composition history makes it a central document of the period's scientific and poetic circles.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously in 1818 with a preface unattributed; authorship established by the 1831 edition, which carries the writer's name and a new introduction, and by family and publisher records.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, January 1818, in three volumes, by Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor and Jones; a revised edition in three volumes with a new introduction appeared in 1831 from Henry Colburn and Richard Bentley. Standard scholarly editions print the 1818 text.

title: The Last Man
description: A forecast of the end of the human species, set at the close of the twenty-first century, in which a plague out of the East empties England, Europe and finally the world. Its narrator, a mountaineer's son raised into the governing class of a decaying Commonwealth, survives every person he loves and outlasts the species itself. It is the boldest of the period's fictions of historical exhaustion, and it was written in the years of immediate personal loss.
plot_or_argument: England in 2075 has abandoned monarchy for a republic of virtue under a philosopher-statesman, and the last heir of the royal house, beloved and accomplished, lives retired with the friend of the narrator's youth. The two are drawn back to public life, to Parliament, to the Greek war of independence and to the courts of Europe, while a pestilence creeps westward from Asia. The plague reaches England, desolates London, scours the continent, and is spread by the flight of nations; one after another the friend, the wife, the children and the statesman die, and the survivor's attempts to raise an asylum in Greece fail. The last chapters follow him alone through a ruined Europe, to a cave and a Sibyl's prophecy, and home to a landscape from which human voice has departed.
narrative_structure: First-person confession addressed to a series of auditors, in three parts with a prefaced 'Prospectus' and an epigraphic apparatus of quotations; the frame of a manuscript of the year 2100 gives the narrative its double perspective of witness and elegist.
principal_characters: Lionel Verney, the narrator; Adrian, the last prince of the fallen royal house; Idris, his wife; Ryland, the poet and friend; the Lady Ryland; Evander, their child
literary_form: Apocalyptic and philosophical fiction; a plague romance and elegy in prose with the machinery of forecast.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a stately, quotation-laden lament, with verse and lyric fragments interspersed and a sustained rhetorical address to Nature.
historical_context: Written in the years after the deaths of a child and of a husband by drowning, and after the collapse of the hopes that the post-war European settlement had encouraged; its republic, its war of Greek independence and its fear of social dissolution belong to the politics of the early 1820s. Its plague borrows the records of earlier visitations and the current reports of Asiatic cholera. It sold badly and was not reprinted in the nineteenth century.
literary_significance: The first great English fiction of total extinction and a founding text of science-fictional eschatology; it reframes the Romantic elegy as the mourning of a species rather than of an individual. Its treatment of epidemic, class and the failure of public virtue has made it a central object of recent historicist criticism. Its recovery in the late twentieth century restored a major work to the canon of the period.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously as by the author of an earlier tale of creation; authorship established by the publisher's records and by family memoranda.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1826, in three volumes, by Henry Colburn; a prospectus had appeared in a literary periodical in 1825; reprinted in the collected novels of 1831-32.

title: The Fortunes of Perkin Warbeck: A Romance
description: A historical romance on the impostor who personated one of the vanished princes of the house of York, and on the fall of that house after Bosworth. The tale treats the pretender as a gentleman bred to a name he never fairly held, and reads the Tudor settlement as the extinction of an aristocratic and romantic order. Its materials are the chronicles, the ballads and the drama that had long handled the same story; its interest is moral rather than evidential.
plot_or_argument: Perkin Warbeck, an unhappy child of a Kentish household, is marked out by a patron of the Yorkist cause, instructed in the part he is to act, and acknowledged as one of the princes believed murdered in the Tower. He is welcomed by the duchess of Burgundy, married to a Scottish gentlewoman while the Scottish king plays the cause for his own advantage, and led through insurrection in Cornwall, through the siege of a northern town and through the mercy of a court he had hoped to inherit. Henry the Seventh's policy narrows about him; he is taken, pardoned, again entrusted and again convicted, and dies at Tyburn, while the romance's closing chapters follow the extinction of the house whose name he wore.
narrative_structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, with ballad and chronicle material absorbed into the narrative and with an epigraphic apparatus; a rise-and-fall structure keyed to the pretender's claims.
principal_characters: Perkin Warbeck; Margaret, duchess of Burgundy; Katherine Gordon; James IV of Scotland; Henry VII; the patron who frames his identity
literary_form: Historical novel and romance; a tragedy of imposture, legitimacy and dynastic extinction.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a formal romantic narrative with quoted ballad and chronicle phrase.
historical_context: Written in the later 1820s, when the historical romance of the previous generation had become the dominant model for fiction on national subjects and when the pretender's story had been revived by drama and by ballad editing. The novel's Yorkist sympathy continues a tradition of dynastic romance rather than the new Whig history. It was published in the year of the French revolution that closed the post-war settlement.
literary_significance: An important late instance of the historical romance by a writer whose earlier fiction had reshaped the gothic tale, and a study of identity, adoption and legitimacy conducted through dynastic material. It supplies evidence of how the school of national romance was adapted to a tragic and feminine moral interest. It is now chiefly studied for its treatment of imposture and of the claims of the disinherited.
attribution_notes: Published as by the author of an earlier tale; authorship undisputed. Not to be confused with the seventeenth-century chronicle play on the same subject already held in this corpus.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1830, in three volumes, by Henry Colburn and Richard Bentley; a Philadelphia reprint in two volumes appeared in 1834.

title: Lodore
description: A domestic novel of education and of the consequences of a father's neglect, following a soldier's son from a romantic youth through an ill-advised marriage and through the separate formation of his daughter. Its running argument is that desire is never satisfied and that character is made by accident unless it is made by principle. It belongs to the moral domestic novel of the 1830s and is one of the last long fictions its author published.
plot_or_argument: Harcourt Lodore, rescued from a wild and dependent childhood, is educated by a kinsman, runs to sea, and at a watering-place is won by the arts of a beautiful woman without fortune or principle, whom he marries against every warning. The marriage, founded on vanity and on deception, dissolves; the daughter is left to the hazard of chance instruction, partly governed by a stern and portionless governess and partly spoiled by indulgent relatives. The middle of the book disperses the family across Europe, and the close gathers the daughter's corrected character, the deaths of the guilty and the marriage of the innocent, into a quiet settlement.
narrative_structure: Third-person narrative in three volumes, alternating between the education of father and daughter; held together by interpolated reflection, letter and maxim rather than by a single plot.
principal_characters: Harcourt Lodore; his wife; their daughter; Hester, the portionless governess; the kinsman who directs the boy's education
literary_form: Domestic and educational novel; a character tale of family dissolution and female formation.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a plain moral narrative with quoted maxim and reflective aside.
historical_context: Written across the years of the author's professional dependence on periodical and novel contracts, and published in the decade of the reform crisis, when the education of an heiress, the custody of children and the law of marriage were matters of active controversy. Its domestic analysis continues the didactic fiction of the preceding generation while abandoning its tale of terror. The unfinished state of its author's papers shaped the text as it appeared.
literary_significance: Closes the fiction of its author's career with the period's most sustained account of the hazards of female education and of the father's failure of duty. It is a significant document of the transition from Romantic domestic romance to the Victorian novel of character formation. Its reading has grown with the recovery of the author's later work.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. One personal name in the family group is not asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1835, in three volumes, with a prefaced argument; reprinted in the collected novels. Certain details of the child's name are left unrecorded here.

title: The Castle Spectre
description: A gothic drama of haunted castle, murdered mother and forced marriage, written for a London patent theatre and built around spectacle, songs and the rising of a spectre from her grave. Its plot of a woman compelled to wed the lord of the castle, and of a guilt that walks the vaults at night, made it one of the most acted romantic dramas of the decade. Its machinery was openly criticised by the new review press while its music and its ghost scene held the stage for a generation.
plot_or_argument: Madeline, the ward of the castle, is commanded by its lord, Osbert, to become his bride, while her attachment belongs to another; the confessor Father Dominic, who has designs of his own on the inheritance, counsels compliance. The castle vaults give up their history: the spectre of a lady murdered in an earlier generation appears, and the secrets of the house, including a concealed child and a dead woman's testimony, are disclosed. Osbert, pursued by the apparition and by his own crimes, is brought to a dreadful catastrophe; Madeline is delivered, the hidden kinship is unravelled, and the drama closes with the exposition of the family guilt.
narrative_structure: Regular five-act drama with songs, chorus and spectacular scenic effects; the supernatural is presented as evidence, and the exposition of the buried history is deferred to the apparition scenes.
principal_characters: Madeline; Lord Osbert of the castle; Father Dominic; Edmund, the minstrel; Alice, the gipsy; the spectre of the murdered lady
literary_form: Gothic drama and musical romance of the patent theatre; tragedy with interpolated song and spectacle.
meter_and_prosody: Verse and prose: blank verse five-beat lines for the serious dialogue, with metrical songs and choruses set to music for the stage.
historical_context: Produced in the season when gothic spectacle was the stock-in-trade of the great London theatres, and when the restricted patents made such machinery a commercial necessity. Its songs, written to be set, belonged to the long fashion for the ballad opera revival. The reviews of the later 1790s, which attacked the play's improbability, mark the beginning of the campaign against gothic stage machinery.
literary_significance: One of the most successful and most attacked of the romantic dramas, and a standard reference for the stage history of gothic. Its handling of the haunted vault and of the compelled heroine supplied scenes and plots to later melodrama. Its reception documents the critical reaction against terror machinery at the close of the 1790s.
attribution_notes: Published and performed with the author's name; no dispute.
bibliographical_notes: First performed at Drury Lane in December 1797; printed in London, 1798, in the acting and reading edition, with the author's name prefixed; music supplied for the songs by the theatre.

title: The Wanderer; or, Female Diary
description: A dark multi-volume tale kept in the diary of a young woman who arrives with no name, no fortune and no protector, and must make her way by her own skill through a world of contested property, forced attachment and concealed birth. It is the most sustained fiction of female independence in the gothic school, and its heroine's competence - her music, her economy, her self-possession - is set against the laws and customs that deny her an identity. Its French and revolutionary material gives the plot its history of dispossession.
plot_or_argument: A woman, landing without explanation in a French port and afterwards passing into England and Ireland, supports herself by teaching and by her performance, and is alternately protected, claimed and pursued by the men she encounters. The diary records her attempts to establish a legal existence, the interference of a bigoted and a designing relative, an attempted compulsory marriage, and the pursuit of an attachment she does not return. Evidence of a murdered man, of a stolen inheritance and of a concealed parentage accumulates through the volumes; the close discloses her title and her kin, but not in a form that restores her peace.
narrative_structure: First-person diary in several volumes, with letters, legal documents and inserted narratives; the heroine's own record supplies both the plot and its continuous moral commentary.
literary_form: Gothic novel and romance of the pursued heroine; a diary-novel of female dependence and property.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; an intense, argumentative first-person style, with documentary inserts and songs performed by the heroine.
historical_context: Written in the closing years of the war, when the law of property, the custody of persons and the narrow employments open to unprovided women were frequent subjects of fiction and of pamphlet. Its use of the French revolutionary settlement and of Irish landed society reflects the same post-Union debates that occupied the national tale. Its title has frequently been confused with another contemporary novel on a similar subject.
literary_significance: One of the most radical gothic fictions of female self-support, and an important text for the study of women's property, labour and legal invisibility in the period. Its diary form anticipates the later first-person domestic novel of constraint. It is now recovered chiefly by historians of gothic and of women's writing.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. Distinguish carefully from the Old English poem and from another contemporary prose romance of similar title held in this corpus.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1814 in a multi-volume format, London and Dublin; no separate first-issue details are asserted here.

title: The Wild Irish Girl
alternative_titles: The Wild Irish Girl; a National Tale
description: A national tale in which an English gentleman, sent to take possession of an Irish estate, falls in love with the daughter of a degraded Irish chieftain and is converted to admiration of a vanishing Gaelic culture. The novel opposes ancient Irish hospitality, music and genealogy to the cold improving landlordism of the ascendancy, and makes the heroine's education and her harp the emblem of a nation's injured refinement. Its romantic union of an Englishman and an Irishwoman is the symbolic settlement on which the whole later national-tale genre was built. It was a sensation on publication and gave its author a European reputation.
plot_or_argument: An heir of English family interest in confiscated Irish lands travels to take possession, only to find the old lord of the tribe living in ruined state with his accomplished daughter in a castle on the western coast. The young Englishman is at first contemptuous, then instructed by the girl in the history, music and hospitality of her race, and won over both to her and to her people's claim. A rival connection with an English relation and the pressure of the ascending family's interests obstruct the match, and the tale closes with a union figured as the reconciliation of the two nations and the restoration of the disinherited.
narrative_structure: First-person letters and journals from the English traveller, interrupted by the heroine's own narratives, songs and Gaelic reminiscences; the embedded Irish tales turn the epistolary frame into an argument about who has the right to tell the island's history.
principal_characters: Horace, an English gentleman with a claim to Irish estates; Glorvina, the wild Irish girl; her father, a chieftain of the old race; an English kinswoman and rival; retainers and harpers of the western castle
literary_form: Prose fiction; national tale; epistolary romance of cultural reconciliation
meter_and_prosody: Prose narrative containing Irish lyrics and simulated translations from Gaelic verse in short lyric measures
historical_context: Published in 1806, in the decade before the act of union had fully changed the politics of Anglo-Irish representation, and amid heated controversy over forfeited estates, the ascendancy's absence and the condition of the Irish poor. Its celebration of Gaelic culture draws on the antiquarian and harp revival of the period and on the travel literature of the western counties. The author came from the Anglo-Irish theatrical and literary world of Dublin and London, and the book was widely reviewed as a political as well as a romantic performance.
literary_significance: The founding national tale and the template for the Irish novel of the Romantic decade, including the historical fictions later written in imitation of it; its marriage plot as an allegory of the two nations is a standard object of postcolonial and Irish-studies analysis. It also established a model of the culturally instructive heroine that shaped European fiction for a generation.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously on its first appearance; the author's identity speedily became known and was acknowledged in later editions. No dispute over authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published in three volumes in 1806, appearing in both Dublin and London that year; the exact imprint sequence is not asserted here. The author's later collected edition and memoirs reissue the text with prefatory matter.

title: O'Donnell
description: A historical national tale built around the recovery of an Irish chieftain's name and fortunes, which moves between Confederate Ireland, the continental Irish brigades and the Scotland of the exiled court. Romance and family injury carry the argument: the dispossession of the Gaelic aristocracy is treated as a wrong whose remedy is honour rather than agrarian improvement. The book is the most openly political of the author's Irish fictions, written in the years when Catholic claims and the union settlement were under active debate. Its use of an early-seventeenth-century setting to speak to present questions is characteristic of the national-tale mode.
plot_or_argument: The son of a dispossessed Irish house, serving in a continental brigade, returns towards his inheritance under the protection of an Irish-born commander, while an English relation and a court faction obstruct his claims and those of the woman he loves. Kidnapping, disguise, a journey through Scotland and the Irish Sea, and a duel bring the injury to public notice, and the closing settlement restores the family name while leaving the larger fate of the nation unresolved.
narrative_structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, with double dating: an early-seventeenth-century main action and a later frame of family tradition; embedded tales and songs interrupt the linear plot.
literary_form: Prose fiction; historical national tale; romance of restoration and exile
meter_and_prosody: Prose narrative with interpolated Irish lyrics and ballad stanzas
historical_context: Published in 1814, at the end of the Napoleonic war and in a decade of contention over Catholic relief, the Irish lord-lieutenancy and the memory of the 1641 and Cromwellian settlements. Its treatment of the Irish brigades and of the exiled Stuarts reflects current antiquarian interest in Confederate Ireland. Contemporary reviewers read the book's pleas for justice to a dispossessed elite as commentary on the union settlement.
literary_significance: Important as the most explicitly historical of the author's national tales and as a case study in the Romantic novel's use of seventeenth-century Ireland for contemporary political argument; its frame of exile and Restoration influenced the later historical fiction of the Irish national-tale tradition.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. The historic chief of the title is a vehicle for the plot rather than a biographical study.
bibliographical_notes: First published in three volumes in 1814, with Dublin and London issues in the same year; the precise order of the imprints is not asserted here, and no reliable statement of composition dates is offered.

title: De Monfort
description: A domestic tragedy in blank verse founded, in the author's own account, on the passion of hatred. De Monfort, raised by a benefactress and in love with her daughter, discovers that the man he has befriended is the son of his father's destroyer, and his settled hatred overmastering every other feeling drives him to kill him in a duel and confesses his hatred publicly. The play's power comes from the analysis of a single passion held up against softer domestic affection, and from its heroine's horrified discovery that the man she loves is an avenger. It was the most performed Romantic tragedy by a woman and a repertory piece for leading actors into the 1820s.
plot_or_argument: De Monfort, adopted in childhood after his father's ruin and death, is beloved by Jane, the daughter of his benefactress, and is bound as well by a warm friendship with the amiable count, whose wife Rezenza had been De Monfort's own earlier attachment. When he learns that this friend is the son of the man whose prosecution destroyed his father, he resolves on revenge yet cannot extinguish his affection, and the strain of the two passions is dissected in long soliloquies. At a public entertainment Rezenza is accidentally shot by De Monfort's hand while he aims at the count, and she dies in a scene of terrified innocence. De Monfort then denounces the count before the company, abandons his love, and gives himself up to justice and despair.
narrative_structure: Regular five-act tragedy with a single ruling passion as its organising principle; dialogue and soliloquy carry the psychological analysis, and the catastrophe depends on a public scene of accidental death and open denunciation.
principal_characters: De Monfort; Jane, the daughter of his benefactress and his beloved; the Count Montaigue, his friend and his father's son; Rezenza, his friend's wife and his early attachment; his old attendant and household dependants
literary_form: Drama; domestic and analytic tragedy of a single passion; closet-originated stage tragedy
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse throughout, with a few rhymed passages for heightened effect; the idiom is conversational and argumentative rather than declamatory
historical_context: Published in 1798 as the second volume of a series designed to delineate the stronger passions, and first played at Drury Lane in the spring of 1800 in a season when regulation domestic tragedy was competing with Gothic melodrama and with Shakespeare revivals. Its psychological method belongs to the late-eighteenth-century analysis of the passions carried on from the moral-philosophical tradition, and its female-authored domestic tragedy responded to the period's debate about women's access to the stage. A celebrated revival with a famous performer in the title role in the early 1820s re-established it in the repertory.
literary_significance: The most influential verse tragedy written by a woman in the Romantic period and a central text for study of the analysis-of-the-passions drama, of the debate between closet and acting texts, and of the nineteenth-century repertory's revival history. Its treatment of hatred as a self-consuming passion has been read as a case study in Romantic psychological determinism.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name in the series title page; no dispute. The play's prefatory argument naming the governing passion is the author's own critical statement.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1798, in the second volume of a two-volume series of plays; the Drury Lane first performance followed in April 1800, and the acting version was altered for the early-1820s revival. Separate critical editions of the play exist; the exact dates of composition of the several revisions are not asserted here.

title: The Vampire; or, The Bride of the Islands
description: A two-act Gothic melodrama of the undead which turned a French stage spectre into the most copied English supernatural shock-piece of the 1820s. A ruined bridegroom and his new love are waylaid on a shipwrecked coast by a corpse-bride who kills the men she has already wed, and the play's machinery of moonlit tombs, animated statues and apparitions gave the English stage its standard vampire iconography. Adapted from a French melodrame, it is nonetheless a shaping original performance in its stage business and its ballad and chorus effects. Its success created a decade of vampiric competition on both London patents and the minor theatres.
plot_or_argument: On a Hebridean coast an English nobleman, deserted by the woman who ruined him, loves a Scottish fisher girl and is opposed by her brother. Wrecks, a burial, and the emergence of a pale bride from her family vault disturb the island: the undead woman claims the living bridegroom, vanishing with him to a spectral bridal. A party of rescuers, guided by a hermit's warnings and by the moonlight funeral rites, breaks into the cavern, the vampire is destroyed, and the living pair are freed, with a moral about guilt and the unquiet dead.
narrative_structure: Melodrama in two acts of continuous scene with songs, choruses and stage business; the plot moves by sensational tableau rather than psychological development, and the supernatural machinery is staged as spectacle.
literary_form: Drama; Gothic melodrama with songs; supernatural shock-piece
meter_and_prosody: Mixed prose and verse, with set songs and choruses in popular ballad and lyrical measures for the supernatural scenes
historical_context: First played in the summer of 1820 at a secondary London theatre whose management was then building a specialty in Romantic melodrama, it belongs to the wave of vampire literature that followed a famous unfinished ghost tale of the same season and its printed and staged issue. The piece drew on French melodramatic technique and on the popular antiquarianism of island superstition, and its imitators on the patent houses in the following decade made it a benchmark of the minor theatre's power over London taste.
literary_significance: The play that fixed the vampire on the English stage and created the conventions of stage supernaturalism later developed in the century's sensation drama; it is a central document for study of melodrama, of theatrical piracy and of the Gothic after the 1810s. Its transmission into after-pieces and into continental repertory makes it one of the most influential of Regency popular dramas.
attribution_notes: Named on the title page as the adapter's work; the piece is an original English performance founded on a French melodrame and its sources are acknowledged in the attribution rather than disputed. Two rival vampire plays of the same year were separately attributed.
bibliographical_notes: First performed at the Lyceum Theatre, London, on 9 August 1820 and published in London the same year; reprinted in the adapter's collected dramatic works, where the text may differ from the acting version. The exact relationship of the printed text to the 1820 playbill is not asserted here.

title: Black-Eyed Susan; or, All in the Downs
description: A domestic nautical drama in which a sailor's sweetheart waits two years at a Deal inn for the man pressed into the service, and is menaced by the shipmate who ruined her brother. The play's celebrity rests on its domestic pathos, its sea-life detail and its final shipboard recognition and trial, with a famous song given to the heroine. It ran for an unprecedented number of performances at a Surrey theatre and was pirated, adapted and re-acted across the country and in America within months. It is the classic example of the Regency domestic melodrama at the height of its commercial power.
plot_or_argument: The sailor William is pressed from the Downs and leaves Susan, the black-eyed barmaid of an inn at Deal, where her father keeps house and her brother's death at the hands of a shipmate is still unatoned. Tom Hatchet, the villain of the same watch, persecutes Susan and prospers by treachery at sea; an American merchant and his suit are interwoven with the lovers' trials. Three years later the ship returns, Hatchet is charged with mutiny and worse, and the courtroom and quarter-deck scenes expose his guilt; William is restored, the villain is condemned, and Susan's fidelity is rewarded with her sailor's hand.
narrative_structure: Domestic drama in three acts moving between a Kentish inn and a ship's deck; the plot is built on separation, persecution and public proof, with the recognition and trial scenes as its designed climaxes and a sententious moral spoken at the close.
principal_characters: Susan, the black-eyed innkeeper's daughter; William, the pressed sailor; Tom Hatchet, his shipmate and her brother's destroyer; Susan's father, the publican; an American merchant; the ship's captain and officers
literary_form: Drama; nautical and domestic melodrama with songs
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly prose dialogue with set songs and a moral in verse; the lyric numbers are in popular stanzas
historical_context: First played in June 1829 at a theatre south of the water that was building its reputation on maritime spectacle and working-class domestic pathos, at a time when impressment, naval discipline and the sailors' condition were live public questions. Its success shows the commercial ascendancy of melodrama over legitimate drama in the later 1820s, and its unlicensed touring and American revivals illustrate the absence of effective copyright protection before the 1830s.
literary_significance: The most performed and most copied melodrama of its decade and the standard case study for the nautical drama, for theatrical piracy, and for the sentimental heroine recast as a working woman. Its combination of domestic injury and professional sea detail made it the model for later maritime sensation and remains the touchstone of melodrama criticism.
attribution_notes: Performed and published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship, though the many pirated and altered country and American versions circulated under other arrangements and titles.
bibliographical_notes: First performed at the Surrey Theatre, London, on 8 June 1829 and published in London the same year in the theatre's acting series; the numerous rival and foreign versions are not collated here. Composition is generally placed immediately before the first performance; no exact date is asserted.

title: Translations of the Letters of a Hindoo Rajah
description: A satirical epistolary fiction presented as the letters of an Indian envoy and his attendants, translated by their interpreter, observing English society, its politics, its literature and its religions on a tour from Bengal through London and Scotland. The oriental point of view exposes the arrogance, inconstancy and self-interest of the British in India, and the ridicule of Anglo-Indian nabob wealth and of fashionable exotic taste is double-edged, since the observer's own superstition is also laid bare. The book was an immediate success and established the writer's reputation. It is the most accomplished of the 1790s vogue of oriental-mirror satire.
plot_or_argument: A Hindoo rajah's embassy, accompanied by his interpreter and his family, travels to England on the business of a disputed succession and a claim for redress against company officials. In letters home the party describes the English constitution, its parties and its pulpit, its theatres, its manners and its treatment of women, while the interpreter's own narrative of an injury in India reveals the mechanism of corruption and ruined families behind the civilising spectacle. The succession claim miscarries, the embassy disperses, and the closing letters report the observer's return and his confirmed contempt for a nation that talks of liberty while oppressing dependants.
narrative_structure: Epistolary satire in two volumes with an embedded narrative by the interpreter; the letters progress from description to argument and are framed by a translator's preface and notes, which allow the joke to be sustained at several levels of narration.
principal_characters: The interpreter-narrator and his family; a young rajah and his counsellors; English acquaintances in London and Edinburgh, including a man of letters and a political orator; a nabob's family in Bengal
literary_form: Prose fiction; epistolary and travel satire with an oriental framing device; fiction of the India question
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; the style imitates formal translated correspondence, with sententious moral reflection and sustained ironic understatement
historical_context: Published in 1796, after the India debates, the impeachment trial of a company governor-general and the regency settlement had made oriental dependency a subject of daily parliamentary and print controversy. The book also answers the decade's fashion for pretend oriental tales and for imitations of a famous Persian translation, and its Edinburgh and London scenes draw on the debate over Jacobin novels and political enthusiasm after the French Revolution.
literary_significance: The ablest of the woman-written oriental satires of the 1790s and an important text for study of British writing about India before and after the impeachment, of the epistolary travel-satire tradition, and of the conservative answer to philosophical fiction. Its framing of translation and interpretation has made it a frequent object of later critical attention.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name, with the translation device as a fictional persona; no dispute over authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1796, in two volumes; reissued in the author's lifetime and in collected editions with prefatory matter. The dates of composition are approximate and are not asserted beyond this range.

title: Memoirs of Modern Philosophers
description: A satirical novel in five volumes which attacks the application of rational philosophy to domestic life, following a family deluded by a philosopher who proposes to live by first principles and ends in ruin. Its target is not abstract argument but its social practice: a father persuaded out of religion and property, daughters reasoning themselves out of decorum, and a community of apostles exploiting the theory for money and seduction. The book was one of the most effective conservative fictions of the turn of the century and helped turn the fashion for philosophical romance against itself. Its comedy is institutional, conducted through clubs, periodicals and boarding-house argument.
plot_or_argument: An easy Scottish laird is converted by a speculative philosopher, whose system of free inquiry removes his scruples about disinheriting his children and about the arrangements of marriage, and who designs a match between his own disciple and the family property. The daughters variously accept and resist the reasoning; a seduction and a flight follow, and the philosopher's party is revealed as a set of interests disguised as principles. The final volumes expose the fraud through a competing clergyman's counter-intrigue, and the restoration of orthodoxy and property is effected by force of ridicule rather than argument.
narrative_structure: Third-person omniscient satire in five volumes, with long dialogues of argument, letters from disciples, and an intrusive narrator who glosses each doctrine; the plot of domestic delusion is sustained over a deliberately slow, encyclopaedic middle.
principal_characters: The speculative philosopher and his disciple; the laird he persuades; his disinherited children and their suitor relations; an apostate clergyman and his family; a boarding-house and periodical-writing circle
literary_form: Prose fiction; novel of ideas and domestic satire; anti-philosophical comedy
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a colloquial argumentative style carrying technical vocabulary of the system under satire
historical_context: Published in 1800, at the height of the vogue for rational philosophy in fiction after the famous novel of justice and after the controversy over the conduct of the philosophical schools. The book draws on Scottish ecclesiastical and Jacobin debate, on the periodical culture of the 1790s, and on conservative alarm at the domestic consequences of infidelity following the French Revolution. It appeared under the author's name and was reviewed as a party work.
literary_significance: A central text of the anti-philosophical novel and one of the most effective fictions of the 1790s campaign against rational dissent; its portraits of a philosopher's household supplied language later used to describe the schools, and it is now studied as a woman-authored conservative novel that helped end the fashion for the speculative romance.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. The philosopher and his party are satirical personae, and the identification of individual portraits with living writers remains unproven.
bibliographical_notes: First published in five volumes in 1800, with London and Edinburgh issues; reissued in the early nineteenth century and in a modern scholarly reprint with introduction. Composition dates are approximate and no manuscript evidence is asserted.

title: Kenilworth
description: A historical romance of the Elizabethan court, built on the tradition that the favourite of a queen secretly married an English heiress and that her death removed the obstacle to his ambition. The novel gives that gossip a fully imagined domestic and political history: a young woman of noble expectations, married in secret and then deserted, is destroyed by the machinery of her husband's design while the court celebrates the queen's progress to a Warwickshire castle. The public magnificence of the entertainment and the private concealment of a imprisoned wife are cut against each other throughout. It is the most purely tragic of the later romances of this series.
plot_or_argument: An English heiress of an old family, persuaded into a secret marriage by an ambitious courtier, finds herself concealed in a distant house and abandoned as her husband's chances at court improve. The queen's progress to the Midlands brings festivals, pageants and reconciliations, while the deserted wife, tended by a faithful dependant, wastes in confinement and is terrorised by an hired agent of her husband's design. Her death, arranged in secret, removes the impediment to the favourite's suit for the queen's own hand, and the closing disclosures expose the instrument of the murder while leaving the courtier's ambition unpunished. The narrative also follows a boy's flight, a pursuivant's hunt, and the old servants of the wronged house.
narrative_structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes; a public court plot and a private domestic plot are conducted in parallel and meet in the last volume, with pageant, festivity and lower-class by-plot used to release and to comment on the central tragedy.
principal_characters: The favourite of the queen and secret husband; Amy Robsart, his concealed wife; Queen Elizabeth; the agent of his secret business; a faithful retainer of the wronged house; a runaway boy and the pursuivant set to take him
literary_form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of court and domestic tragedy
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a courtly and ceremonial diction for the progress scenes, contrasted with homely Scots and west-country speech in the domestic chapters
historical_context: Published in 1821 and founded on the Elizabethan gossip and chronology surrounding a famous favourite, the queen's progress, and the mystery of a gentlewoman's death, material then being reworked by historians and antiquaries. The romance belongs to the second great phase of the series which had remained anonymous, issued when its author's public fame was established but his name still withheld, and written in the depressed years immediately after the war with France.
literary_significance: The standard example in English fiction of the Elizabethan court romance, and the most quoted treatment of the rumoured murder of a secret wife; its progress and pageant chapters are a much-studied instance of the historical novel's use of ceremonial spectacle. Its reconstruction of a domestic tragedy inside a court history made it a source for later plays, ballads and pictorial treatments of the legend.
attribution_notes: Published as the work of the author of the Waverley romances, whose name was still withheld; the attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London, 1821, in three volumes; the first edition was issued from the author's own press arrangements and reissued many times in the series and in standard collections.

title: The Talisman
description: A romance of the Third Crusade which sets a fanatical and magnanimous English king beside a generous and sceptical Saradin leader, and makes the mutual respect of the two warriors the moral centre of the book. An English knight of disowned Saxon lineage, whose vows and his mistress's commands bring him to the East, serves unknowingly under the very king who despises him, while a talisman of supposed protection becomes the instrument by which reason and tolerance are shown to work. The book is the most deliberate of its author's apologies for civility across the line of faith. It was published with a companion tale of the same period in one series.
plot_or_argument: A Christian knight of an injured Saxon house, bound by his mistress's command to wear a relic and to forbear battle, attaches himself to the English host in Palestine and is taken into the service of the great commander of the opposite faith. The two chiefs meet, are saved and instruct each other, and are brought into conflict by the jealous ambition of the knight's own patron and by an injured lady's suit for protection. The relic proves in the event to be an innocent object whose supposed virtue worked only by the courage and courtesy it taught, and the tale ends with reconciliation between the enemies and the knight's restoration to his mistress and his line.
narrative_structure: Third-person romance in three volumes with a continuous single hero's career, framed by chapter epigraphs from older plays and ballads; the argument is carried by set-piece interviews between the two great captains rather than by intrigue.
principal_characters: The English king of the Crusade host; the great commander of the Saracen camp; Kenneth, a Saxon knight in disguise; the lady of an English house whose suit he defends; an ambitious courtier patron of the hero
literary_form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of the Crusades
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre, with quoted lyric and dramatic epigraphs in ballad and song measures at the head of chapters
historical_context: Published in 1825 with a companion tale of the Crusading period, it belongs to the vogue for Crusade romance revived by the antiquaries and by travelled knowledge of the nearer east. Its plea for courtesy across religious difference reflects the liberal moment of the Catholic and civil-relief controversies then in progress in the British parliament, and the book's oriental chivalry draws on the contemporary translation of Arabic history and poetry.
literary_significance: The clearest statement in the series of the romance of toleration and of the exemplary meeting of enemies, and a much-anthologised source for nineteenth-century ideas of chivalry and of the East. Its treatment of a false relic as an instrument of moral teaching makes it a central text for study of the author's handling of superstition and enlightenment.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name now disclosed in the general title of the series; no dispute over authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh, 1825, in three volumes, issued with the accompanying dedication and with the author's name; frequently reissued and included in the standard collected editions.

title: The Adventures of Quentin Durward, Captain of the Guard of the Scottish Bow
description: A historical romance of the court of France at the end of the reign of Louis the Eleventh, seen through a young Scottish archer of the king's bodyguard of the Scottish Bow. The book's interest is political: a patient, ironical king who hates the state of his own nobility is opposed to a great vassal of the league of the Public Weal, and the private fortune of the Scottish soldier is entangled in the quarrel over an heiress whom the two princes would each use. The chase, the ambush, the siege of a prince's city and the trial of the injured heiress supply the incident. It is the most completely wrought of the French romances of the series.
plot_or_argument: A young Scottish gentleman of a ruined house obtains a place in the king's archers of the guard and is at once employed in a dangerous private errand. His mistress, an heiress of the borders of France, is courted by a powerful neighbour of her father's blood and threatened by an allied prince, and the Scottish captain's protection of her brings him into the king's policy and into the league's hostility. The king's agents and the prince's soldiers dispute the city, the heiress and the succession, and the archer's fidelity through ambush, imprisonment and siege is rewarded at the close with his mistress's hand and the recovery of his own fortunes.
narrative_structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, following one hero's advancement through a court and a military quarrel; the political argument is carried in long interviews with the king, and the plot in pursuit, concealment and the defence of a city.
principal_characters: Quentin Durward, a Scottish archer of the king's guard; Louis the Eleventh; the great duke of the league; an heiress of high birth and her injured family; a kinsman suitor of power and violence; retainers of the Scottish bow
literary_form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of the French court
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a formal and courtly idiom for the French chapters, with a Scots and border speech for the hero and his countrymen
historical_context: Published in 1825, it was written after a journey on the continent which put its author in possession of the French towns, castles and archives used in the tale, and it depends on the histories of the league of the Public Weal and of the king's destruction of great vassal power. Its Scottish bodyguard of the French king reflects the antiquarian knowledge of the Auld Alliance then being recovered by Scottish historians, and its picture of a patient political king answers the statesmanship literature of the post-war decade.
literary_significance: The model example of the court intrigue romance in the series and a standard source for the nineteenth century's idea of a shrewd, ironical king working against feudal privilege. Its treatment of honour and interest through a soldier's loyalty made it a school and library favourite, and it remains the most frequently read of the French tales.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh, 1825, in three volumes; reissued in the series and in the standard collected editions, with the author's later revision and prefatory notes.

title: The Fortunes of Nigel
alternative_titles: The Fortunes of Nigel; or, Nigel Olifaunt of that Ilk
description: A historical romance of the reign of the first British king, in which a poor young laird of a Scottish house goes up to London to prosecute a claim at court and is thrown among the money-lenders, goldsmiths and players of the Jacobean capital. Its subject is the fortune of a dependent and a kingdom: a Scotch estate, a pawned jewel, a court favourite's malice, and the cause of an injured house which the king must finally judge. The romance is the most concentrated study of the new British politics after 1603 that the series contains, and it treats the transaction of land for money as the real event of the age. Its London topography and its portraits of a famous king and a famous goldsmith have been much quoted.
plot_or_argument: A young Scottish laird, sent to London to secure the repayment of a debt owed to his house by the crown, finds his estate threatened by a court favourite, is arrested for debt, and is befriended by a goldsmith of the Exchange whose credit and whose household he endangers. A diamond pledged and lost, a suit of wrong, a duel, and the protection of the king himself carry the cause from the counting-house to the council, and the Scottish claimant is finally preferred while the favourite is discountenanced. The lower world of London law-writers, actors and money-lenders carries on the same argument in the by-plot.
narrative_structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, with a single hero's cause as its spine and a fully realised urban by-plot; the king's conversations and the goldsmith's house supply the two poles of the design.
principal_characters: A young laird of a Scottish house; King James; the goldsmith to the Exchange and his household; a favourite of the court who wrongs the Scottish family; a law-writer, actors and money-lenders of London
literary_form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of the Jacobean metropolis
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; Scottish speech for the hero and his countrymen, and a city idiom of trade, law and the playhouse for the London chapters
historical_context: Published in 1822, it uses the removal of a Scottish court to London after 1603 as a study of the union in practice, of the crown's dependence on merchants' credit, and of the favourites and suits which then determined fortunes. Its treatment of a king famously wrote, argued, and favoured supplies a political anatomy of the early British state, and the tale's money-lending and pawnbroking world reflects contemporary debate about credit, debt and the opening of professions to those formerly restricted.
literary_significance: The most important of the series' romances of the British union and one of the earliest historical novels to make credit, pawn and legal suit the motive force of its plot. It is a standard document for the study of the representation of London, of Scottish migration to the English capital, and of the fiction of money in the 1820s.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh, 1822, in three volumes, with a dedication and the author's prefatory account of the historical matter; reissued in the series and in the standard collected editions.

title: The Absentees
description: A novel of Ireland immediately after the act of union, whose subject is the withdrawal of the Irish gentry and their dependants from the country to the English metropolis. The book follows a family of the county and its tenants through the miseries produced by absence, by the desire to be received in London, and by the ruinous expense of a fashionable exile. It is the most directly political of the writer's Irish fictions and was read from its first page as a commentary on the union's consequences. The comedy is social and the argument is economic.
plot_or_argument: An Irish county family, its hopes raised and its fortunes unsettled by the union, removes to London to purchase acceptance and to place a daughter in the marriage market, while the estate at home is governed by agents and falls into confusion. A younger relation left behind in Ireland sees the mischiefs of exile and of the borrowed money that maintains it, and the family's pretensions are exposed by a successful rival connection. The tale ends with the recognition that a family and a country are ruined by spending their income elsewhere, and by a settlement which keeps one branch of the house at home.
narrative_structure: Third-person social novel in three volumes, alternating an Irish county plot with a London plot; the narration is brisk, illustrative and openly argumentative, with the writer's own political reasoning framed by the story.
literary_form: Prose fiction; novel of manners and political tale of the union period
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a plain conversational style with Irish and metropolitan speech used to mark the two economies the book compares
historical_context: Published in 1812, a generation after the author's first Irish tale and within a few years of the union, when the departure of the Irish parliament made absenteeism an immediate public question. Its subject matter is the London Irish social season, the agent-governed estate, and the debate in the periodicals over the economic consequences of union. The writer's own position as a celebrated Irish author resident between London and the Longford estate gives the book its double point of view.
literary_significance: The first sustained novel on absenteeism and the union, and a key text for the study of Irish fiction between the 1800 act and the Famine. It supplies the economic argument that the later Irish novel made its central theme, and it remains a document of Anglo-Irish social history as well as a piece of fiction.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published London and Dublin, 1812, in three volumes; reissued in the author's collected tales and in modern reprints. The order of the Dublin and London issues is not asserted here.

title: Patronage
