description: A novel of church and state patronage, following three young men who must be provided for in a world where office, living and rank are distributed by interest rather than by merit. Its argument is institutional: it examines the machinery by which preferment is given, and measures the corruption it produces in families and in the professions. The plot turns on an illegitimate son's claims and on a father's anxiety for the education of dependants for public life. It is the most programmatic of the writer's English county novels.
plot_or_argument: A man of family interest undertakes to advance his dependants and his natural son by means of patronage, and the three several careers of church, law and the army are tried against each other and against the demand for principle. Marriages of interest, a concealed relationship, and the discovery of a family claim disturb the plan, and the preferment sought by interest is in the end awarded on a different footing. The closing settlement defends the reformed use of patronage while exposing its abuses, and the education of the young men is the true subject of the book.
narrative_structure: Third-person omniscient novel of institutions in three volumes, with paired household plots, long explanatory dialogue, and an openly argumentative narrator; the design is illustrative rather than suspenseful.
literary_form: Prose fiction; novel of manners and institutional comedy; the county novel of opinion
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a plain didactic style, with speech patterns marking church, law, army and trade
historical_context: Published in 1814, during the last years of the war with France and at a moment of vigorous controversy over church patronage, pluralities and the sale of offices. Its county and metropolitan scenes reflect the post-war competition for professional advancement, and its treatment of a natural son's claim belongs to the period's debate on family obligation and property. The writer's own experience of the Irish estate and of London literary society supplies both its practical knowledge and its reforming purpose.
literary_significance: An important early novel on the machinery of patronage as a social system, and a document of the reform argument that the century's institutional novels continued. It is read chiefly for its analysis of professional advancement and of education for public life, and it stands beside the author's Irish tales in the history of the novel of social institution.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1814; reissued in the author's collected novels and in modern reprints. The volume count and the order of the first issues are not asserted here.

title: Harrington
description: A novel of the education of a spoiled only child, and the writer's most serious study of the formation and the unlearning of prejudice. The boy is made irrational by indulgence and by a tyrannical schoolmaster, and the book then shows how the habits of a generous nature are recovered through shame, friendship and the example of suffering. Its central and most discussed passage is an embedded tale of an injured Jewish family, which converts the boy's unreasoned contempt into a lesson on the persecution he has himself helped to inflict. It was the last of the writer's major novels and is the most explicitly moral in purpose.
plot_or_argument: An only child of a weak father and an indulgent mother is tortured at school by a brute master whom his family will not believe against, and his character is warped by sympathy denied and by flattery accepted. He is rescued and educated by a plain-spoken friend of his father, whose method of honour and reason restores his judgement. The middle of the book is taken up with the history of a money-lender of the wronged faith and of his daughter, whose injuries at the hands of the boy's own family expose the cruelty of a prejudice inherited and never examined. The young man's life is then governed by reparation, by a friendship tested in illness, and by the choice of a wife whose worth he is at last able to recognise.
narrative_structure: First-person autobiographical fiction in three volumes, looking back on a boyhood and young manhood; the embedded tale of the injured family interrupts the forward movement and reframes the whole education as an argument about prejudice.
literary_form: Prose fiction; novel of education and moral reformation; the autobiographical child-narrator novel
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a plain, reflective first-person style, changing from the speech of an injured child to the measured idiom of an examining adult
historical_context: Published in 1817, it belongs to the post-war debate on the civil condition of Jews in Britain, to the controversy over classical schooling and the punishment of children, and to the writer's long engagement with the education of judgement begun in the family's educational books. Its plea for the recognition of a persecuted minority is a direct answer to the treatment of Jewish characters in contemporary romance, and its school chapters draw on the reports of English academies of the period.
literary_significance: A founding text of the English novel of childhood and of the literary argument against religious prejudice, and the writer's last important fiction. Its embedded tale is a standard document for study of writing about Jews in the Romantic period, and its first-person education design anticipates the nineteenth-century novel of development.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1817, in three volumes; reissued in the author's collected tales and in modern reprints with introduction. The volume count of the first issue follows the bibliographical record; the order of any simultaneous Dublin issue is not asserted here.

title: Falkner
description: The last completed novel, a study of a man haunted by an accidental death and of the education of a girl committed to his charge. Falkner, whose prosperity rests on an inheritance obtained after the death of a benefactor whom he unwittingly caused, places his ward under the protection of a family of high character and loves her in silence, while the secret of his conscience presses on him until disclosure. The book is quiet, domestic and almost entirely free of the machinery of its author's earliest fiction, and its interest is the patience of guilt and the cost of renunciation. It closes a series of novels on maker's responsibility and desertion.
plot_or_argument: A gentleman of broken fortune, carrying the secret of an accidental death which gave him his ward, educates the girl he has injured and loves, and watches her attract a suitor of her own class. A rival's malice, a mother's disappointment and a marriage made against inclination try the household, and Falkner keeps his secret until his health and hope fail. The confession, the marriage and the death of the woman he loved and of the man who loved her bring the tale to its close, with the surviving child the only promise of repair.
narrative_structure: Third-person domestic novel in three volumes, narrated with a restrained, reflective economy and a single concealed cause running beneath the household surface; it opens with a brief history of the hero's earlier life.
principal_characters: Falkner, the man of the secret; Margaret, the daughter of the family whose death he caused and his own ward; her mother; a suitor of her own rank and his family; a rival of malice and interest
literary_form: Prose fiction; domestic novel of conscience and renunciation; the novel of education
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a plain, reflective and unornamented narrative style, with quoted lyric at the chapter heads
historical_context: Published in 1835, in the decade of reform and of the new poor-law and factory debates, it belongs to the author's long later career of editing, biographical writing and domestic fiction. Its subject of conscience, guardianship and the education of a dependent girl reflects the period's literature of moral responsibility, and its quiet realism marks the distance from the philosophical romance of the 1810s in which the series began.
literary_significance: Important as the closing novel of a career that founded two prose traditions, and as evidence of a movement from Gothic and philosophical romance to domestic realism. It is studied for its treatment of concealed guilt and for the relation it sets up between its author's earliest and latest fiction.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1835, in three volumes; reissued in modern editions with introduction. The date of composition is not documented here beyond the year before publication.

title: Thoughts on African Slave-Trade
description: A short polemic against the slave trade and against the argument that commerce in human beings can be regulated or excused. Its reasoning is applied philosophy rather than feeling: the trade is shown to rest on the same violation of private judgement and of person which the writer's political theory had condemned, and the pleas of property, of climate and of gradual amendment are answered one by one. It belongs to the renewed abolition campaign of the 1820s and is the writer's most direct intervention in a live parliamentary question. The pamphlet is argumentative, lucid and unhedged in its conclusion.
plot_or_argument: The trade in enslaved people is examined as a system of law and interest rather than as a scene of private cruelty, and the writer contends that no regulation can alter the nature of a claim to property in a person. The apologies offered for the trade - that it is sanctioned by long usage, that the condition of the enslaved is improved by service, that abolition would ruin commerce and endanger the colonies - are each tested against the principle that judgement and the person are not transferable. The argument closes with the claim that emancipation, not amendment, is the only consequence consistent with the principles of justice, and with an appeal to the public and to the legislature to act on that principle.
narrative_structure: Continuous short argument in a single pamphlet compass: statement of the question, examination of the defences offered for the trade, and a positive conclusion addressed to the legislature and the public.
literary_form: Polemic and pamphlet; applied moral and political philosophy addressed to a public question
meter_and_prosody: Prose, no metre; a plain, closely argued style of the philosophical pamphlet, free of invective
historical_context: Published in 1823, when the renewed abolition movement was pressing the question of the colonial slave populations before parliament and when the writer's own political reputation had lasted a generation. It answers the amelioration argument of the period's colonial writing and draws on the reports and speeches of the renewed campaign. It belongs to the literature of emancipation between the abolition of the trade and the acts of the 1830s.
literary_significance: A significant document of the abolition campaign of the 1820s and of the application of philosophical anarchism to a live political question. It is read now as part of the literature of slavery and emancipation, and as the late political writing of the circle out of which the period's radical fiction came.
attribution_notes: Published as the work of a named author of the philosophy of political justice, whose identity was indicated on the title page; the attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1823, as a single pamphlet; reissued in the writer's collected political and philosophical tracts and in modern collections of abolitionist writing. Publisher and format of the first issue are not asserted here.
